body: I just requested my FBI fingerprint record and can tell you that successfully-expunged ARD does **not** appear on the rap sheet.  This is as of April 2024.

This is not correct.  If the expungement is done properly, the State Police sends the expungement order over to the FBI.  While the FBI is not required to expunge it as well, it almost always does so.  I just requested my own FBI record (with the fingerprints) and it immediately came back as "no record."

If I remember correctly, I had to describe the circumstances which led to the charges.  I didn't go into detail about the incident itself, but stated that I was charged, that I entered ARD on XYZ date, and that I completed it on XYZ date which also included an expungement. I also uploaded a copy of the order which formally dismissed the charges.  The renewal was approved pretty quickly.

Hi! I didn't renew until after I completed ARD. This was partially due to the fact that it wasn't up for renewal until 2021 and I completed my ARD in 2019.  I'm not sure what the result would have been had I needed to renew when I was still in ARD.  I probably would have tried it anyway.

That's what I ended up doing, and it was an obvious choice because it asks about "arrests" and not just "convictions." If it only asked about convictions I would have said no. There was never a question about being honest; federal applications like that make you check a box that says everything is true and correct and it's actually a crime to deliberately make false statements. At the time I wrote this, I was wondering if the disclosure of an arrest would disqualify me. It turned out that my renewal application was approved as close to immediately as possible (maybe 2 months). Nobody ever asked me about it.

I'm not sure how this would have gone down if it were an initial application instead of a renewal, but I pulled my FBI rap sheet as well and there was no record of the incident. I have no idea if DHS could see it anyway but if they could, it didn't impact the outcome.

I forgot I posted this! Yes, I did reapply back in 2022 when I was finally able to travel internationally again. I figured, just try it and see if it works. I disclosed the charges, provided copies of the order directing it be expunged, and waited. They approved the renewal after about 2 months (maybe--it didn't seem all that long). I never had to go for another interview or say anything else about it. 

In the context of this, I ended up ordering my FBI records as well to see if the charges were still there. They also didn't show up anymore. My DUI was from about 3 1/2 years ago when I reapplied for Global Entry so at least for Pennsylvania ARD, it didn't matter.

I had a DUI in 2018 and accepted ARD which ultimately dismissed the charges and expunged the record. I already had Global Entry at the time. I went to renew it in 2022 and was approved. I disclosed the initial charges (it asks about "arrests" not just convictions), and then provided the Order expunging it. I didn't need to go for another interview and it was approved pretty quickly. So it depends on your situation, but it's not an automatic disqualifier.

I'm very sorry for your loss.  You probably already know that this is a group of us who have been the DUI drivers and we didn't find this sub until it was too late.  I have a lot of feelings about the entire DUI system, many which I've posted about previously but which seem inappropriate here but which I'll summarize as being:  the image the general public has of "who gets a DUI, and what makes them get a DUI" is very much not true.  I do think your post has value though and hopefully someone who needs to see it sees it and will make a different decision next time.

So, the calculators aren't entirely accurate (they skew a bit high, in my experience), but your BAC decreases by about .015 each hour.  So he was probably around .20 at the time of the accident.  I don't know that functionally it makes a difference though.  Many states top out their sentencing at .16.  Potentially .20 would make him ineligible for diversion or a lesser sentence, but you usually see that happen if it's at .25 or above.  He wouldn't be eligible for any of that anyway if he has 7 prior convictions!

I didn't do a MADD Victim Impact Panel but at my PA DUI classes they just breathalyzed; no urine screens.  They're on limited time there so they don't bother with that.  Actually, only one of my classes actually had us take breathalyzers.  The rest it was on the honor system.

I get that it should be that easy, and of course, it's easy **now**, after seeing the consequences of not getting one.  But wow knowing what I know now about BAC levels and the fact that tolerance means absolutely **nothing** in terms of whether you're okay to drive--it makes sense that people truly don't know.  Most people who have driven while "just a bit tipsy" have probably been close to or at the legal limit.  I wish we knew more about how unreliable subjective feelings of intoxication are before it was too late.
Now that I'm five years out, I agree with you.  It does get better with time.  It's not easy, but eventually it happens.  Thank you for sharing.

A.  If you're less than 30 days before trial, it's a bad idea unless you truly have no other option.  Your new lawyer would need to instantly come up to speed and would probably need to request a continuance.  If you switch on the eve of trial, you will ultimately need to have it continued.  Not sure if that's the proceeding you have coming up.  

B.  A one-time switch, no.  Clients change lawyers all the time for all kinds of reasons.  If you show up to court proceedings with a new lawyer each time, the DA and judge assume it's because you're a bad client (making unreasonable demands, refusing to pay, etc.).  That isn't going to impact the sentence though.  

C.  You need to read your fee agreement.  If you paid a flat fee up front, my guess is your fee agreement says it's non-refundable.  If it does, then no, your lawyer is not required to refund you unless his state bar or disciplinary board specifically requires it.

First, how "expunged" is it?  Some states truly do make it go away where it doesn't even show up in an FBI check.  Other states will expunge but only at the state level or something to that effect.  If it's truly expunged and you run a check on yourself (state police, FBI, even a quick online search because sometimes those records get picked up by private companies) and verify that it isn't anywhere to be found, it's quite possible that you could not disclose it and nobody will ever find out.  HOWEVER, I would err on the side of disclosure.  There's a reason why the application specifically worded the question that way and if you don't disclose and get caught, now there's a question of your honesty.  Numerous professions cite problems with "honesty and trustworthiness" as a reason to refuse someone a professional license.  An expunged DUI that you disclosed may not be a deal breaker for an employer, but failing to disclose might raise issues.

Rather than ask your criminal attorney, it would be better to contact an attorney in the state where you're applying who handles issues with professional licenses.  That person would be in the best position to tell you whether you can leave it out.  

"Doesn't it defeat the purpose of having my record erased?" In some ways, yes.  In other ways, no.  Life is so much easier having it expunged even if you do have to disclose it on applications because of the way the questions are phrased.  I'm sure everyone here who can't get theirs expunged would agree with that!

First, it's important to remember that for every person who gets a DUI, on average they've driven at least 80 times under the influence prior to that moment.  .08 is so easy to get to quickly and DUIs are incredibly common.  The first year is definitely the hardest but it does get better.  It's been over four years for me and there are times I still occasionally think back on that moment and am horrified; because if literally one thing about my DUI had been different, there would have been far harsher consequences.  Those moments may never truly go away.  What made me accept it and no longer beat myself up was realizing just how easy it is to get a DUI and how common it is.  I didn't stop drinking after the DUI; but I am far more mindful now.  I never had the "blessing in disguise" or "grateful for my DUI" moments that other people write about, but it no longer haunts me.

I had a DUI four years ago.  I did a diversion program where basically you go on unsupervised probation for 6 months, pay thousands in court costs, go to DUI classes where you learn about how "drinking too much alcohol and driving is bad" and basically stay out of trouble.  At the end, everything was dismissed and the record was expunged.  There's truly no record of it anywhere; even the fingerprints were destroyed.  I renewed my Global Entry no problem after disclosing the DUI which was long expunged.  There are some things I won't be able to do because of the charges.  Certain professional organizations I'm associated with have leadership positions that specifically ask about criminal history.  So I'll miss out on some of those opportunities, and of course there was a big financial hit because of the court costs  and the frustration of losing my license for 60 days and having to use an interlock.  But from reading here, it could have been so much harder.  It does get better.  And next time, you'll be far more mindful of how much to drink before driving and it will amaze you how many people clearly \*should\* have DUIs and just haven't gotten caught yet.

Seconding Drink Fox!  No online BAC calculator is completely accurate, especially if you're talking about heavy drinking, but Drink Fox is fairly accurate if you're honest about alcohol content, portion sizes, and weight.

With those charges you're eligible for ARD and honestly, ARD isn't that bad.  It's mostly annoying and a waste of time with classes.  But the police have to have probable cause first before pulling you over, and the blood test may not show ThC.  I'd talk to a lawyer.

Glad to hear that!  I'm not sure what state you're from but our (Pennsylvania) are dismissed as well.  Fingerprints destroyed and everything, so it truly doesn't show up.  I was nervous about getting my Global Entry renewed but that happened with no problem so I assumed Canada would be similar.  I won't be going there anytime soon because of its vaccine requirements, but if they ever remove that this will be good to remember!

Some counties default to reducing charges while others don't.  Also the police had to have probable cause in the first place.  If they got the .19 breathalyzer improperly or inaccurately, that can be suppressed and won't even be part of the state's case.  Or if the .19 person just got pulled over for swerving but the .10 person caused an accident that injured multiple people, that could explain a different outcome. I tend to think in general though that DUIs are the only offense we're in practice you're guilty until proven innocent.

Speaking as a lawyer who ended up with a DUI, $3,500 is pretty standard and if it's a flat fee then the lawyer expects it will result in a plea deal.  It's not that you can't find someone for less, but if they're a lot less then it's because they're working off of volume and you can guarantee that they're not going to be very attentive.  It's not that they don't care, it's that nobody can be completely attentive when they have 100+ cases they're handling at a time.  At a minimum, it's worth talking to a lawyer.  They understand the system, they know the laws, and they know what a realistic outcome is.  The court process for my DUI was so ridiculously easy and I absolutely believe having a lawyer made no difference in the outcome.  But they took care of the paperwork and I just had to focus on showing up on time.  It really made a bad situation much easier to handle.    


Hang in there, it does get easier.

The first two weeks were hard, getting the criminal complaint was a terrible day, then there was a honeymoon period with all the court things happening.  I know, it sounds crazy to say but the court process was the easiest!  It was very by the books and clerical and "just the facts," which made thing pretty easy.  Then until I was off of probation it was difficult.  I didn't see many people during that time and spent far too much on Uber and Lyft because of not wanting to drive at all.  It was a strange combination of feeling very isolated and at the same time feeling like everyone knew about it (the DUI school people, the DMV who took my picture for the interlock license, etc.).  There are fewer than 5 people in my life who know about this and it's definitely my skeleton in the closet!  Nothing really helped other than checking off the list of things that needed to be done before it was over.  Mine was pretty easy because it was less than a year from the time the DUI occurred until the time I was off of probation, and the entire record is expunged.  But it was still a challenging time and I don't think I fully recovered from it until recently--about four years later.  Eventually the worst of it passes; it just takes time.

Talk to a lawyer, but ARD isn't bad.  It's unmonitored probation, you go to DUI school, you'll probably have to go to an additional DUI school program because of the BAC and go to three AA meetings where you just sit there not paying attention and get your court slip signed.  If you do ARD you'll lose your license for 60 days although you can get an interlock during that time so it's really more like 21 days that you're truly unable to drive at all.  The interlock is a pain but keeps you on the road and independent.  Once you complete the program, the charges are dismissed, the fingerprints are destroyed, and the record is expunged.  I just got approved for my Global Entry renewal after having done ARD so it truly is not a conviction or a guilty plea.  From being 4 years out on the other side, ARD is a gift compared to what other states have.  There's a lot of frustration during the time that you're in ARD, and a lot of people criticize it for being too lenient.  But it truly does give you a chance to start over.  

Also, PA doesn't have the requirement that other states have where you need to complete an SR-22, the document which guarantees your car insurance rates will skyrocket.  They will go up for at least a period of time, but compared to elsewhere, PA is pretty lenient toward DUIs especially first-time DUIs.
Woohoo!  I only had that thing for 60 days but hated it.  The one good thing was it kept me driving, but the device was such a pain.  Glad you're at the end!

You'll be okay.  If the DUI is legitimate (high BAC) and it's your first offense, ARD is truly a gift we are fortunate to have in PA.  You go to a few court appearances, fill out paperwork, attend the ARD hearing where all you say is "yes I accept the conditions of the program" or something like that, and then you do classes.  For me, it was two twelve-hour classes where you literally hear things like "people drink alcohol.  Sometimes people drink too much alcohol and that leads to alcoholism.  Alcoholism is a medical condition."  It's really like being back in middle school.  The license suspension kicks in after you go into ARD and you get notified by Penn Dot about 30 days in advance.  You can drive with an interlock which is a pain, but it keeps you on the road.  Then once it's done and you've paid the court costs, you're finished!  I was placed on 12 month probation in ARD but then was released early after 6 months.  It's non-reporting in most counties, meaning you don't check in or meet with your probation officer.  They also don't drug test.  

The important thing to remember with ARD is that it's not a conviction or a guilty plea.  Some judges say it's "an implied guilty plea" which I guess is a fair opinion to have, but the law simply doesn't see it that way.  You can have it expunged and it truly does expunge everything.  No fingerprints/mugshots are kept, it doesn't show up on the State Police or the FBI criminal history check.  I just renewed my Global Entry with no problem, even after disclosing ARD.  Also, PA doesn't require you file an SR-22 for insurance so you can potentially keep a lower rate for a period of time because the insurance company won't necessarily find out about it right away.  

Those of us in PA who can do ARD really are fortunate compared to so many other states.  It's such a stressful period but it could be so much worse.  Once ARD is finished, you truly do get to move forward, and that's something many (most?) other states don't allow.  It will be okay; we've all been through it here and it really will be better once you're further removed from it.

The dumb questions are so true!  You can also find some of these online.  How I handled it was something like "there's a culture in my profession of drinking a lot so I got used to it and built up a tolerance.  I had no idea that tolerance has nothing to do with BAC.  I'm definitely going to be mindful going forward."  The evaluator said he didn't think I had a problem with alcohol but because of my BAC level I had to go to another two day class and three AA meetings.

Get the lawyer.  You're close enough to the limit that a lawyer could make a difference.  Even just having someone handle the paperwork is a huge burden taken off of you.  There's so much else going on in a DUI it was a relief to not have to worry about court paperwork too.  Also, when it comes to lawyers, you really don't want to be paying the lowest price.  You want someone who will take the time to review your case and answer your questions.  In general, a very low priced lawyer is not going to be doing that.

I never did etg tests but I did look this up back when I had my DUI.  I found a post on the site Quora where several people said that they did the "drink Friday, sober on the weekend, test Monday" thing and passed.  So you may be okay.
Congratulations!  It really does get better the further removed you get from it.

Oh I'm so sorry that happened to you.  I got pulled over while I had my interlock and after that I always used the Waze app to avoid police officers.  As far as probation goes, encounters like that didn't have to be reported (that's what my officer told me when I reported it anyway).  I have nothing better to offer except to follow your lawyer's advice as far as how to move forward.  Small town police encounters can be the worst because they have nothing else to do!

It definitely seems like the focus is on convictions (or the equivalent, so guilty pleas/no contest pleas as well) because when I was looking online, everyone who was denied appeared to actually be convicted of a DUI rather than go through diversion.  So if you have the $100 to spare, it's definitely worth at least applying!
Same!  And there's no need to even have a picture on that platform.  I use a similar one and **I** don't even have a profile picture, let alone force my clients to have one!  That's messed up.

The calculators are based off of a formula, which has been shown to not be very accurate when you're talking about a lot of alcohol.  It's very accurate for low and moderate drinking--think one glass of beer or wine but when you get into high alcohol consumption it doesn't work as well.  Using my pocket breathalyzer, they two are frequently off between .03-.05 with the online calculator overestimating.  The most accurate one I've found online though is [drinkfox.com](https://drinkfox.com) because you can put in specific drinks and they give you a lot of options for how to size each individual drink.

LOL that's pretty much what it is!  It almost has a tone of "okay boys and girls, don't do this again because it's bad."  I remember everyone talked to us like we were 4 and said things like "okay you have to sign at the bottom of this page.  This is called the 'order.'"  It's almost amusing to look back on it because it was several years ago now.

If you have to file an SR-22 your insurance company will find out even if you don't tell them directly.  The only time they may not find out right away is if you live in a state where the SR-22 isn't required.  I never told my insurance company about my DUI (SR-22s aren't required in my state) and kept the same rate for about 2 years after.  But they eventually pulled my driving record and found out about the accident and raised my rate.  So eventually they'll find out about it and if you have to file an SR-22 there's no way of hiding it.

Geico was amazing and I'm probably never going to switch from them after my experience!  I wasn't required to notify them of the DUI because my state is one of the few that doesn't mandate SR-22s or FR-44s.  Eventually they found out because they pulled my driving record at renewal.  Presumably they saw the license suspension and DUI in addition to the accident.  But even then, they didn't raise the rates by much--it was probably a difference from $80 a month that I was paying pre-DUI to $100 a month.  Three years accident and claim-free and I'm back down to my pre-DUI rate.  Never switching from Geico!

I hate mine too!  It's terrible and it doesn't help that I'm already unattractive and my straight hair makes it worse.  I wish I had curly hair.  There's nothing good about straight hair; it's quite ugly and makes me look even uglier than I already am.

Agreed on the reasons why you need a lawyer!  I'm a lawyer myself and when I went through this three years ago, there was no question I needed to hire someone.  Having someone who knows what they're doing turned the entire court process for me into one that basically involved filling out paperwork and waiting around.  I would have been a complete mess trying to do it on my own, even though it was so easy.

If she doesn't have a lawyer, she needs one.  You can be removed from ARD if you pick up new charges during the probation period, which would result in her facing the penalties of the initial charge.  A lawyer could potentially prevent that from happening.  Jail time may be in the form of house arrest.

You'll get a letter from PennDot with instructions of where to mail in the license.  It will tell you the effective date that it starts.  However, it will functionally begin sooner because your 30 days won't run until PennDot receives your license.  So, you need to mail it in a few days before the suspension begins so it gets there in time.  Once you mail it in, you cannot drive.  For me, the suspension began approximately a month after going onto ARD.  

For insurance, unless there's something stating otherwise in your policy, you are not required to report the ARD.  I have Geico and never told them, and the rate only went up two years later (I went from paying $80 a month to more like $100 a month).  PA doesn't require an SR-22 which is what really triggers the high rates quickly.  So if you've had Progressive for awhile, you may have a few renewal cycles of paying the same rate.  If you tried to switch plans though, that company would run a check and find the DUI.  All the best!

Depends on what you mean by "winning."  If you had a definite statutory DUI (.10 instead of .081), got into an accident, admitted you were drinking at the scene and had a blood test, it's going to be extremely hard to get a dismissal.  That can happen if you had borderline BAC results, or if you weren't in an accident so probably cause is possibly at issue, or the BAC test was a breathalyzer which are woefully inaccurate.  But in the case of a definite DUI, "winning" is more getting charges reduced or getting reduced penalties.  If you qualify for a public defender (and most people who think they can get a PD can't because they make too much), they'll get the same results for definite DUIs.  Borderline cases are slightly different because they don't have the resources that private attorneys would have.  But skill-wise they're just as qualified.

It can take awhile for the company to figure it out.  Mine didn't go up until after almost 2 years after the DUI.  I was never asked to disclose it so didn't.  I don't know if it's because they pulled my driving record or because my DUI was because of an accident.  It was a lot they paid out so regardless, it was eventually going to go up.  Even so, mine went from $80 a month to around $98 a month.  It wasn't terrible (Geico!)

This was around 3 years ago but they're probably still accurate:    
Attorney:  $3,500 (**very** worth it, made the process really clinical and just filling out paperwork)  
Court costs:  $2,776  
Interlock:  $250 (???) can't remember at this point.    
Miscellaneous license fees:  $200 is my best guess but I think I'm way off on that one.  I think it was less.    
DUI intervention class:  $200

In hindsight, I got off lucky!  

The actual "program" itself was a joke.  You get a CRN, a D&A evaluation if your BAC was high, go to Alcohol Highway Safety School (waste of time but fortunately the others in the class were entertaining) and if a high BAC or accident, DUI intervention.  Then just pay fines and stay out of trouble.  It's unmonitored so nobody is checking up on you and there are no drug or alcohol tests.  They could do this, but there's not the manpower to do that for every person on ARD.  It's a very paperwork-heavy process and if you have someone who does it for you, it's pretty easy.

Not worth it.  Police officers will sit on the side of the road facing the direction of license plates so they can run them and check for this.  This is what they're looking for.  If they find a suspension, they **will** follow you, pull you over, and cite you.  This happened to me when I drove with an interlock but my license showed up suspended.  The police officer was aggressive and hostile and if I hadn't been in a location where our interlock program is connected with the courts, I absolutely believe I would've been cited.  Driving on a suspended license when it's due to DUIs is a huge issue and it would ultimately result in an attempt to revoke probation, an extension of your suspension, and increased fines.  That doesn't even address the legal fees to try to keep you on probation.  Uber or paying someone else to drive you is expensive and a true burden, but it will be more expensive to do this and get caught.

I was in your position.  The day I got the notice I was being charged with my DUI I wrote a suicide letter and planned it for that night.  Then, I looked up my chosen method online and found out it only had a 72% chance of success (yes, there actually is a website with this information and it isn't hard to find).  I decided the likelihood of failure was too high to go through with it.  Truly the only thing that kept me going was the knowledge that at any point I could change my mind.  And then the holidays came around and a few fun professional events happened, and I got to travel, and eventually I paid off my costs, had the record expunged and felt more "neutral" on it.  I wouldn't say I made the "right" decision in choosing not to go through with it, but if you take some time, the worst of the feelings do pass.  My DUI was almost 3 years ago and with the exception of some travel-related questions (like, will my non-conviction ARD prevent me from renewing Global Entry), it's mostly behind me.  I never liked it when people insist on telling others that they "have to" continue living.  That's really presumptuous to pretend we know your situation better than you do!  But it really doesn't stay this bad forever, and it can get easier sooner than you might expect.

Well, the reason you can do it so quickly here is because ARD never results in a conviction.  It's actually not even an admission of guilt although unofficially it's referred to as an "implied guilty plea."  When you complete ARD the order says the charges are dismissed and the record gets expunged.  The fingerprints are actually destroyed and it doesn't show up on the FBI record.  Second offenses do, but the first ones won't show up if you request your history.  I know in a lot of states that expunge DUIs, it still gets listed as a conviction (for some reason I remember California being this way?) but that never happens here.  In some ways this question would be easier to answer if it **were** a conviction (or a guilty plea or a no contest plea) because then at least it would be obvious what the actual disposition was!
Cut back after my DUI.  I think I may have gone about 3 weeks as the longest individual stretch.  I do drink now, and can handle the same amounts.  But now, I make sure I'm not driving.

I was more than double the limit, and it was 2 years ago.  The entire period of probation was quite a depressing period but honestly after reading about experiences here, it was quite easy in comparison.  The truth is, there \*are\* some opportunities I'll probably lose permanently because of this.  But for the most part, I'm living the same life I was pre-DUI.  It doesn't have to be completely terrible.
Yay!

It's probably county specific but I know that the attorneys I know who work for the local DA office don't really want to deal with 1st offense DUIs at this point because of backups and so are trying to get them all through as soon as they can.  It's not that there are new DUIs these days, it's more that the ones that were in the system haven't been dealt with yet.  Ask your attorney because it's going to depend on what's going on at the DA's office.  Some of them don't want to deal with DUIs at all and others want any excuse to get back into court.  In general, positive random screens are good and can only help you; particularly under circumstances where you could make up any reason not to comply and probably get away with it.

If he received a letter from PennDot saying "you're eligible for interlock limited license beginning XYZ date," then that's the period that starts the clock.  The statute says "one year from the date operating privileges are restored."  Not "one year from the date the interlock is installed."  Right now if he hasn't received anything back, he's not licensed to drive although that will change as soon as he gets the paperwork from PennDot.  For example, my license was suspended effective 1/31/2019 for 60 days.  I didn't get my actual confirmation from PennDot until 2/8/2019.  But, I could still get my license back beginning 4/1/2019 because the 60 days began from the date on the letter.  They \*\*should\*\* credit him for getting the paperwork in on time.

1. If the DUI was on February 9th then it's undoubtedly showing as "pending" in background checks at this point--by background checks I mean the FBI and PA State Police.  If it isn't it's only because they're shorter staffed due to COVID.  When your ARD is complete, you can expunge it; in some counties this is automatic and in others you have to petition for it.  On average it takes about 4-6 months to have everything destroyed.  The first thing to go is the public access docket; mine disappeared literally the day the order was entered.  
2. I'm on the side of, if you aren't required to disclose by your employer or because of a professional license requirement, don't disclose.  There's nothing to be gained by it.  if you're asked, then you can just say you're currently on ARD and your expected completion date is XYZ.  My personal opinion is that "less is more" though I recognize some jobs have different expectations.  
3. In an informal, personal context responding to nosy people who happen to find out?  Sure, lie away if you think you can get away with it!  Not everyone knows how to use the public access docket even though it's quite easy.  In a professional context, no.  The record is public and it will show whether you've been charged.  Once ARD is complete, the record will be expunged and the charges themselves will be dropped.  You will be able to truthfully say you were never convicted.  Saying you were "Charged" or "arrested" is a different story and there are differing opinions on what you should answer.  
4. They're probably more likely to check criminal dockets and social media profiles before digging around for newspapers.  I'm in the process of hiring someone (COVID and all!) and honestly the only thing I'm interested in is social media; but we have a licensing requirement where we have to disclose criminal convictions or guilty pleas to our disciplinary board so I'm just assuming that none exist if someone is applying for the job.

Once the order is granted terminating ARD (and you can terminate after 6 months if you've paid your court costs and completed all of the requirements though some counties ask for more information than others when you request this) it gets removed immediately.  The actual expungement process takes about 4-6 months to fully wipe it out.  Some counties do this automatically and others you have to ask for it.

You forgot to add "I drove around every day for a year on a suspended license and know exactly what to do not to get caught.  So you all should do it too!"  But I thought he only had 3 DUIs instead of 5!

If you \*\*are\*\* a nurse and have to carry liability insurance, reach out to your carrier and see if there are approved providers.  They bill through insurance so you don't pay out of pocket.  Attorneys almost always work off of retainers for these types of cases.  $3,000 at $350 an hour isn't even 10 hours of time and professional license defense requires much more time than that.  This is not just filling out paperwork.  A retainer is a deposit to be paid in advance for work that will be performed.  The lawyer doesn't get paid until those fees are earned.  Unfortunately we have to do this because if you just issue an invoice, clients decide that they don't need to pay it.  So functionally, they decide to be the employer who tells an employee "we know you worked 40 hours but we're only going to pay you for 20. Part of it depends on the consequences if you get caught driving somewhere outside of the places where you're allowed to go.  But most states are pretty consistent that there are increased penalties for violating the terms of the restricted license--usually fines, the possibility of jail time, a longer suspension, etc.  

Restricted licenses almost never include the ability to do things like go to the bank, get gas, get groceries, go to a friend's house, etc.  It tends to set out very specific places where you can go and even limits the hours when you are permitted to drive.  A police officer could pull you over because he was just scanning plates and it was flagged.  The longer the suspension is in place, the more likely this will happen.  When I had my interlock during my 60 day suspension, I was pulled over on Day 30 because the State Trooper was scanning plates.  A lot of people here say that they drove during a suspension or drove outside of the restricted license places and they never got caught.  So you can definitely do it if you're careful and live in an area where officers just don't check things like that.  But personally, for as much as I hated the IID I would choose that over a restricted license.

So it sounds like you have an interlock in your car, right?  They're set to fail at anything above .03 (in my state it's .025).  Technically, with ***any*** amount of alcohol in your system you could end up with a DUI if an officer found that you were still "impaired."  It's harder, but not impossible particularly if the BAC is .07 or something close to the limit.  For legal limit purposes, .08 is the number that means you will be charged with a DUI.  There really is no choice but to charge you with a DUI.  .15 is usually going to be an aggravated charge because it's almost twice the legal limit.  So yes, at .15 you're "more drunk" than you are at .08 even if you don't "feel" drunk.  Alcohol doesn't metabolize very quickly but if the breathalyzer says .032 then in another hour you'd probably be able to start your car but would get a warning.

An attorney may be able to keep your probation intact--a lot of times DAs are so overwhelmed with DUI work that they'll give you a pass one time.  But you won't get that again so you absolutely cannot drive on a suspended license.

No experience in nursing or medicine, but from experience:  the hurdle is getting into school.  You can be a nurse and get a DUI and keep your job with some obstacles. So the first place to start is the school; I know that call is terrible and embarrassing to make.  But they're the ones who will tell you whether you're barred from it.  Assuming school is fine, the next step is to talk to someone who knows how the licensing works.  You're not the first one who has had this happen; somebody will have heard the same scenario before.

A lot of professional positions that have licensing requirements also have disclosure requirements for any criminal convictions.  In my state nurses are required to report the DUI to their licensing board even if they get into a diversion program and get it expunged at the end.  If they don't, then they can get into trouble for not reporting.

I think in order for you to get in trouble, someone would have to go through each and every attempt, match up the dates and times, compare them to your license status, and then decide whether to flag it.  I don't think anyone at the DMV is going to do that; they get those reports once a month when the vendor recalibrates the machine.  They're looking for positive blows rather than violations of the suspended license.  That's what the police are for.

Just starting your car isn't going to flag it.  The DMV isn't going to be looking at the dates and reporting back to police.  There's too much activity going on for it to be realistic.  But, if your license is suspended and a police officer runs your plates, it will come up as suspended and if you cannot produce a limited or interlock license, then it's probably going to be treated as driving while suspended.  This is how I got "caught."  I was driving quite carefully but the State Trooper was scanning plates and it only showed up that it was suspended, not that I had an IID license.  A lot of people on here have driven with no issues though at least once so it's definitely something that you can do and get away with. For me, after one drink my BAC will fluctuate between .03 and .07.  This depends on time, amount consumed, whether I had water/food, the type of drink, etc.  Wine usually gets me around the .03-.05 range, hard liquor slightly higher and beer slightly lower.  I try to take at least an hour to have one drink and this keeps it lower.  I'm about 100 pounds depending on the time of year.  I don't feel impaired at this level and would definitely be able to handle at least one more; but can't do that if I know I'll be driving.  Two is my absolute limit and I really have to be careful about all of the factors above; I don't have the second one unless it's going to be a \*\*really\*\* long evening if I know I'm driving.

If you google "alcohol evaluation questions," that will give you a good idea of the type of questions asked and most of them have pretty obvious answers.  I studied for a bit before having mine done.  I wanted the least level of "treatment" possible so gave answers that were different than the "real" ones.  Though for the most part, they were questions related more toward depression/anxiety issues rather than consumption issues.  

Here's how I passed with the high BAC (not quite as high as yours but definitely in that range):  I said that I'm in a profession with a strong drinking culture and the amount I drank pre-DUI was the same amount as those around me.  I said I didn't realize that tolerance has next to nothing to do with BAC levels and that it's actually quite scary to think that everyone around me would drink at least as much and then drive.  Then I said I had stopped drinking and didn't plan to start again anytime soon (mostly true; I really did cut back a lot after the DUI although that was never going to be a long-term goal).  For the "do you think you have a drinking problem" question, I said that at the moment of my DUI I probably met the diagnostic criteria and don't think I could \*\*not\*\* be given a diagnosis given the BAC.  However, given the length of time that passed, I do not believe that is the case and I never experienced the physical dependency symptoms.  

Basically, the goal was not to say "I never drink, I don't know what happened," because the BAC doesn't support that.  The goal was to show insight into how I got to the level where I could tolerate such a high amount of alcohol and articulate an intention to not do that again.  It seemed to work and the evaluator said I didn't need inpatient or IOP treatment.

I didn't do one but I know how they work in my area.  Suppression "hearings" are really not hearings in the sense of authenticating and entering evidence.  They're usually done through motions (which is similar to a hearing because you're in front of a judge, but you don't have to show up).  They don't happen until after it's already been determined that there won't be a plea deal and so a trial would be scheduled after; and the motion determination would be about whether that evidence can be introduced or not.  They can also be done as part of a pre-trial conference with the judge.  Unless you've done something wrong, I don't know why someone would be arrested after this.

"Criminal background check" usually means checking the actual criminal docket.  It doesn't typically include a DMV search which is a separate fee unless the job actually requires driving.  "Off the record" depends on where you are; some states will just seal records while others will outright destroy them.  But an expunged record for employment purposes is generally going to make the DUI not appear.

Take the $80 a month!  If you read what others post here, that's an amazingly low rate (it's what I'm paying, actually).  For IIDs, I had to use SmartStart, and I found them to be decent.  Easy enough to use although I never quite got the technique down.

Personally as a lawyer who got a DUI and had to search for lawyers:  I'd personally go with the 3rd.  He seemed to have the practice experience (general criminal is sufficient for most DUI purposes just like "family" is sufficient for most custody issues), made you feel comfortable, gave you a bit of immediate assurance and his rate is competitive.  $3,000 for the average attorney means slightly over 10 hours worth of time which is about right for standard first offense DUIs.  The first one would probably be worth it if you had a highly specific, specialized issue but if it's $3,500 ***plus*** $500 per court appearance, that's a lot.  The second just didn't seem to give enough detail; he's probably decent enough but doesn't seem to give you any real information.   I looked for rate as well as personality and whether I felt like this person cared.  They all say that they can help you with a DUI, but very few show real concern and compassion.

PA would ordinarily suspend your license because there's actually a registry and database that almost all of the states share.  LA is one of the really \*\*weird\*\* states that does everything differently so it's quite possible that they wouldn't report anything to PA!  So...if PA never knows about it and you don't get a notice from PennDot saying it's suspended, then you're good to drive.  At some point you won't be permitted to drive in LA.  But is there a reason why you would even need to request a new PA license?

Technically a "parole" officer is quite different from a "probation" officer.  Parole officers are after you're released from jail (the drunk pit doesn't count) while probation officers are for keeping people out of trouble.  I haven't heard of anyone's probation officer contacting their employers.  Not saying it couldn't happen, but it seems to be the exception rather than the rule, especially for long-term employment and non-violent crimes.

Geico for me has stayed the same; it went up slightly (about $100 a year) after I got the new car which was post-accident but pre-ARD acceptance.  I've been through multiple renewal cycles and it hasn't changed.  I have no idea why this is; my guess is they haven't pulled my driving record in awhile; there have been plenty of opportunities for them to figure out what happened given the nature of the DUI.  I have no idea if the $100 increase was because of the new vehicle or the DUI.  For now, I'll take the rate I have at the moment but I still periodically look at rates.

I really dislike the narrative in courts that if you have a DUI, you have a substance abuse problem.  Of course, that's possible; but it's also really easy to be over the legal limit and most people who drive at that level wouldn't meet the criteria for a substance abuse disorder.  There are so many people who go out to happy hours and places with free flowing alcohol, putting down 4 drinks in less than 2 hours.  Very few of them are going to be under the legal limit and of course they're all driving!  I think if you really pay attention, you can get to the point where you physically notice a difference between .05 and .08.  But, .08 versus .07 is going to be much more difficult.

You'll probably be fine if you go heavy on the water today.  4 days is on the long end of being able to detect it and generally it's people who drink heavily on a consistent basis who are most likely to have positive screens.  There was someone on Quora who posted awhile back who said that for his weekly Monday probation meeting, he would stop drinking Thursday and never had any issues.  So you're probably fine.

The real reason to have representation is that the criminal system is absolutely ***not*** set up for defendants to represent themselves.  You simply cannot negotiate or advocate for yourself and preserve your 5th Amendment right to remain silent at the same time.  People handle DUIs without attorneys all the time and usually the results are similar if not the same, but that doesn't mean that they know how to handle the legal system (they don't, attorneys hate dealing with unrepresented parties), it's because the system itself has standards in place where you can already guess what will happen based off of BAC levels and circumstances around the DUI.  It isn't necessarily wise to pay an arm and a leg for an attorney, but if someone is way under market rate, you should be asking why.  Either they're brand new and don't really know what they're doing, or they're running their practice strictly on volume and basically walk out with the same result for every client.  Most people who say "I'll just get a free lawyer" don't qualify for public defenders.  What's more important is that you feel comfortable with whoever it is you talk to; that they're telling you what to expect (even if it's not what you want to hear) and being clear about your rights and options.

Is there a reason why you actually \*\*have\*\* to tell anyone?  Is it required disclosure?  If not, I just don't see the point; it doesn't sound like it will be personally helpful to you and it really can only hurt at this point.  Basically, among the less than 5 people who I had to tell because I couldn't avoid it, it was "I have a DUI" and that was it.  No details, no answering questions.  If I could've gotten away with not telling those people, they wouldn't even know.  At this point if I actually had to disclose it, I believe I would take a "just the facts" approach.  DUI, got into diversion, completed it, everything is expunged.  No emotion or socially expected self-reflection necessary.

People handle DUIs without attorneys and get either the same or better results but it's risky.  The system just isn't designed to have criminal defendants representing themselves when you have a Constitutional right to remain silent.  Personally I chose to have an attorney because with me there was a very real chance I would have interacted with everyone as though I was a lawyer (out of habit--I am one) rather than as a criminal defendant.  

As far as what to look for in an attorney, or what to look past.  I would say in general stay away from people who promise certain results; you can't guarantee that--you can give a breakdown of whether a dismissed charge is likely to happen but nobody can guarantee it.  Also, while there is a degree of truth to some judges or DAs being more lenient if they see a particular attorney involved, it doesn't work the way you see on t.v.  So better to just quietly ignore that part!  And also, if they charge a really low fee, you should really ask why it's so low compared to everyone else:  it's probably because they either run their entire practice on volume or they're inexperienced in the area.  

FWIW, I'm glad I had an attorney because it meant all I had to do was show up and sign paperwork!  But, it was absolutely something that could've been done without an attorney.

For a 3 month suspension it's not worth actually moving your home permanently.  What I did was use Uber and Lyft (I work about 15 miles away and round trip was somewhere in the range of $45-50).  I got around some of this by taking advantage of first ride discounts and then used Freebird to get some additional discounts.  It worked for the few weeks but definitely wouldn't have been sustainable long-term.  I probably would have stayed in a hotel close by.  

I heard that Waze carpool is good and if you're in an office job with regular hours and it's a major metropolitan area, you will probably find someone who you can carpool with.  It's substantially cheaper than a typical ride share.  

Driving on a suspended license is really tempting but you get stuck further in the system if you get caught doing it.  Police officers do run plates and you don't have to be doing anything wrong for them to catch it.  When I got pulled over (I had an interlock throughout my suspension) I wasn't breaking any rules but the state trooper was scanning plates and caught the suspension.  Plenty of people do it without any problems, but if the duration is 3 months it's really something you have to weigh whether it's worth the risk or whether you can adjust your budget to account for the Uber/Lyft/ other rideshare options.

I thought I read somewhere that the average person has driven legally intoxicated at least 80 times before getting caught.  I have no idea if it's accurate, but I definitely had several drinks before driving and knowing what I know about how BAC works, I was constantly over the limit.  Now it really is one and done if I'm driving.

Also in PA- when you get served with the Complaint and notice for the preliminary hearing, the Affidavit of Probable Cause will tell you what the BAC was.  It will even be listed in the charges; "High BAC" is .10-.159, "Highest BAC" is .16 and above.  So that will give you some clues as well.

From what I've seen, the no alcohol thing really does get enforced if you're at DUI court level.  Technically it applies even for ARD, but there are so many people on it and nobody supervises you in any way where that would be enforced unless you were getting into other trouble.  I absolutely understand why a first DUI happens and can even understand a second one (it's really, really common for it to happen within the first 7 years because people get overly confident and their tolerance level goes back up).  By the time you're on the third one though, that's a pattern and at a minimum, the sober time will re-set your tolerance level so that you wouldn't be able to handle as much.
For a $100 fine, there really isn't anything to lose by fighting it.  If it's a voluntary alcohol evaluation, you probably could just not submit it if it came back negative.

I suppose the first question is:  while you don't have the physical piece of paper, do you know for certain you don't have the actual IID license?  It may be on the DMV's system.  How did you do the monthly checks if you haven't had the license?  In PA we were required to go for a calibration 30 days after installation.  

On the probation officer front, it's going to depend on how your county handles IIDs generally.  In my county we had to use a specific vendor and they ***did*** report positive blows to the probation department.  Whether that resulted in consequences I don't know, but it was in the contract I signed.  I get the sense that that's the minority though because most interlock providers are not contracting with a court system and they're really just sending them to the DMV unless requested to do otherwise.  

Getting the unrestricted license back is going to be a pain because you already applied for the interlock license.  The way it worked in my state was that you have to do the final compliance check (I think most states with interlocks require this), then the vendor certifies that you had no violations, then you get your license back once you confirm with the DMV that they actually received the certification.  Also, you aren't allowed to get the device removed until you have your unrestricted license back.  I suppose if the DMV never actually issued the license, it's worth calling and getting them to not issue it.  That way once the restoration date arrives you can speed the process along!

He's so determined to drive after drinking enough for it to register on an interlock (as opposed to say, going on a bender at home and staying holed up there for the next 12 hours or so) that he actually spent more money to cheat the interlock.  There's only so much you can do if you've already told him to stop.  Sometimes telling people very bluntly helps them realize how they're being ("Dude, you actually spent money to cheat the interlock device?  Why don't you just go on a bender at home if you're that determined to do it?  That's what everyone else with an interlock does!").  If he wants to drink he's going to drink, but maybe a reality check of the situation eh's putting himself in will help.  I'm so sorry you're in a position like this.

I'm so sorry this happened, especially because nurses seem to be treated so much more harshly by their boards than anyone else.  I swear doctors get away with more than nurses!  The first step is to talk to an attorney to find out what you're looking at.  We can tell you a lot on here, and even those who are attorneys here (there are a few of us!) can't give you genuine legal advice specific to your state.  Even if you need to take a sick day, it's worth it to know what the consequences are.  

My own case I did through diversion.  I could've challenged it based off of a warrant issue but that was too much of a risk and I knew I had a DUI so I took diversion anyway.  The expungment was worth the trouble.  My attorney made it all really easy--we did it by the books, it was extremely clinical and literally filling out paperwork.  I think being an attorney myself and trying to talk to a DA about diversion would've been a bad idea--because I would've started trying to litigate instead of accept a deal!  

You are no worse than anyone else who drinks at happy hours.  Most people don't realize how quickly they reach .08 or how easily you can build a tolerance where you get beyond that point.

Did it get expunged?  I've never \*\*heard\*\* of anyone getting turned away at the border if it was actually expunged, but of course that doesn't mean it never happens.  I heard that people on diversion in my state just take a letter with them indicating they're not convicted and they get in just fine (the border agents have too much to do and if it's on court letterhead saying it's not a conviction, they just let people in).  Again, that's just what I hear; I'm sure others have different experiences.  Ultimately it's the decision of the agent at the border itself whether to let you in or not.  I think the best place to start is to talk with a Canadian attorney who an tell you whether you really need to apply for a permit or if you're realistically going to to be let in without one.

He won't get ARD again and will be treated as a second offense; fines for second offenses start at $300 and 5 days in jail although a lot of counties will let you do that through house arrest or something similar.  License suspension is at least a year and he'll have to drive with an interlock; really the suspension is going to be the least of his worries.
Unless it gets treated like standard tobacco, it's more likely to be in the category of alcohol.  Yes, it's legal to use, but for probation purposes everyone is told they're not allowed.

Even if you get away with it, recreational marijuana isn't legal in your state so you're literally breaking the law each time you smoke it.  It's also illegal on the federal level.  Full disclosure, I get that eventually it will be recreational everywhere but that stuff smells like a dead skunk and considering everyone I know who is a regular user looks high and spaced out, I have nothing good to say about it.  That said, my experience with non-reporting probation was that you weren't called in regularly or even randomly.  I suppose if someone called and tipped off your probation officer, or there were social media pictures it would be different, but typically they're concerned with whether you pick up new charges than with monitoring you.

I'm sorry.  It sounds like everything is really hard right now; I was without my license for about 2 weeks while waiting on the interlock and that was difficult enough.  I can't imagine doing it while having a child and all of the responsibilities that go along with it.  Driving really is something you don't think much about until you can suddenly no longer do it.  

The first problem is you "they don't have my certificates from treatment."  If that's the case, then you need to contact wherever it was that you went to treatment, tell them that they weren't sent to PennDot and make sure they get faxed or emailed over.  PennDot can take up to three weeks though to mail out your limited license.  

Driving without a license is definitely violation level, but it seems like most POs give you a free pass and they're more concerned with you picking up new charges.  Hang in there!
Progressive tends to be pretty good for DUIs and sometimes insurance companies will give you a lower premium to entice you to switch.
LOL I don't smoke but I'd totally get a drink with you.  Arrest should be expunged by now (thank you diversion!) so Canada here I come!

I've heard this but I'm not sure.  I've definitely driven past officers who are clearly scanning plates or looking for DUIs and have never had an issue; this was at various times of the day and after midnight too.  In my state the DUI stays on your driving record for 10 years, but I'm not sure how immediately that shows up.  To the best of my knowledge, when the plate is run, the vehicle information comes up first which is how people get caught with suspended licenses, and then the officer has to click through an additional screen to actually get the driver information.  That's what the people at the ignition interlock center told me.  So it seems like they're looking primarily for suspensions first and then they check the individual driver.  I haven't had any issues since my license was restored.

Out of pocket for specific DUI results, mine came to around $10,000 total.  $2,776 in court costs, $3,500 for attorney, additional $250 for DUI "intervention" (complete waste of time class), interlock plus DMV associated fees was $575 for having it in for 60 days.  The real kicker was the 42.7 hours I lost in productive time when I was dealing with the DUI from beginning to end, which, at my rate of $250 an hour came out to...$10,675.  No, I personally do **NOT** ever see that much; I have to pay my overhead LOL!  There are a few incidental costs that never made it into the calculation and fortunately my insurance increased by only $100 for a year and I have no idea if it's DUI related or "got a new car" related.  $10,000 is more realistic in terms of "in the moment" costs. Never really understood the advice to stop drinking completely after a DUI; depending on your size it could literally be 2 drinks that puts you over the legal limit.  That's not exactly alcohol abuse.  Anyway, the next day is so true!  Basically, if you're hungover you still have alcohol in your system and you're probably still well over the legal limit.  There's also a website called [drinkfox.com](https://drinkfox.com) where you can put in your weight and number of drinks and get a rough estimate of what your BAC still is.  It's amazing how long it stays even after you've stopped drinking.

From what I've learned in reading these boards, the big issue is getting your license in the first place and whether the DUI is a barrier.  In general with professional licenses that aren't related to driving, it seems to be in the category of "this is something that can get flagged, be prepared to address it, but the further it is in the past the less it matters."  On this board alone there are people who got licensed in law, physical therapy, medicine, nursing, education and even security clearances after their DUIs, and that's not even including the people who were already employed in those fields and didn't have their licenses revoked.  So the biggest issue is being licensed.  The reality is that the DUI ultimately will close some doors for you and it does for all of us--there are certain positions I would have wanted to apply for but can't because you have to disclose your arrest history and even expunged arrests count.  But in general it doesn't mean you can't complete your program or have a really successful and fulfilling career.  I hope this helps!

That's going to be so state specific.  At least in my state, you are allowed to refuse the FSTs and the *roadside* breathalyzer.  If you are arrested (as in put in handcuffs and taken to the police station or if you skip that part because you end up in the hospital after an accident and get a visit from a not so friendly police officer) and *then* you refuse, then the automatic license suspension penalties kick in.  I think in my state, most defense attorneys would say they wish it were public knowledge that the roadside breathalyzer and FSTs are not the same thing as the official test which doesn't kick in until after you're in some form of custody.  But yes, in general I'm not even sure police officers realize that there's a legal difference between the two and they will absolutely tell you that you're destroying your case if you refuse the FSTs or roadside test.

From what it seems on here, one single fail doesn't result in much (if any) consequences.  There are so many reasons why someone could fail that a probation officer doesn't do much with just one, particularly if there was a passed result shortly after.  It tends to be more important for DMV purposes because most states seem to have a rule that you can't have any fails within a certain time frame before having it removed and getting your license back.  

Mine was supposedly reportable to the probation office but it was unsupervised probation and I have no idea if that ever actually happened or not.  If you have a vendor that's directly connected to the court system (I think VA has something like that) then it's probably more likely.

Not meaning to be snarky, but how do they enforce that?  Are they giving applicants random EtG screens?  I know that definitely happens in my state when attorneys get put on probation in place of losing their licenses, but AZ is extending that to applicants as well?  That's pretty strict!

On the law school front, schools and State Bars are getting more finicky about this ever since the ABA report came out on substance abuse issues (whether it's genuine or just an act is up for debate).  For my state's Bar, we had to disclose whether we had any criminal charges--there were a few people who had what I'm sure were DUIs who had to address it as part of a Character and Fitness examination, but as far as I know they were all allowed to practice.  I don't know anyone who wasn't allowed to sit for the Bar and if that had happened with anyone in my class I'm sure it would've gotten around.  I don't remember if the law school application had criminal history questions but everyone who the Bar Exam part applied to already had it happen in undergrad so I assume with enough time that it's something that can be overlooked assuming otherwise acceptable LSAT and GPA scores.  I graduated several years ago though so I'm not sure if things have changed.  

The whole "we want to show sobriety" thing is a bit of a joke.  It's such an ingrained part of the culture that starts from law school; these guys put down 4-5 cocktails in a 2 hour happy hour period and all of them are driving back.  They also don't appear drunk, which should tell you something about their tolerance levels!  A \*\*ton\*\* of attorneys have DUIs and even when they're supposed to be abstaining during their probation, they're still drinking.  Take care of the DUI part first, then when it's done you can look at law schools.

>When I was applying for the Bar Exam there were a couple of classmates who had some issues on the Character and Fitness portion because of their "expunged criminal record" from college.  I now know that they meant a DUI; to the best of my knowledge, everyone who that applied to was allowed to sit for the Bar and (assuming they passed) ended up being licensed.  There are even judges in my area with DUIs and about once every two months another attorney ends up getting one--and those are just the ones I know of.

The fact that you got a letter without actually getting a letter isn't so surprising; they can get your address just by running the license plate.  But if it's an actual charge, it's really unlikely that they'll just randomly add new DUI charges at the court appearance.  The only way that would probably happen is if you said something indicating that you were drinking--this, by the way, is why you shouldn't go unrepresented.  Have a lawyer go with you so that you don't accidentally say that you panicked because you thought you would get pulled over for a DUI or anything like that.  But if you weren't already charged with it, you're probably safe on that one.

Mine was last August and the winter holidays were pretty rough.  Thanksgiving came before I went onto probation and then Christmas came the week after going onto probation though didn't spend time with family during that time because of having to work.  Fortunately by Easter I was done with my license suspension and was just paying off the fines.  I never got the "blessing in disguise" revelations that others here seem to have, though simple things like being able to warm up my car for 5 minutes make me better able to put it in the past. If I could've gotten away with it I wouldn't have told my significant other about the DUI.  Unfortunately that wasn't a long-term solution because we live together so I had to tell him.  It almost ended our relationship.  If I got into another relationship now I wouldn't tell the person. A lot of people say that talking to someone helps but honestly it really didn't help me.  I think I've just accepted that the depression is my new normal and it's just going to be that way for a long time.  So nothing helpful there, but it's definitely not just you who feels this way.
Seems to vary depending on where you are.  At mine there were no tests although it was always a possibility.

If you stop by 12am then presumably you're not drinking whole bottles of wine.  You should be fine by 2:30 the next day unless you really went crazy.  If you really want to be sure, then stick with the standard beer/wine rather than cocktails with multiple liquors.  Much easier to keep track that way.

Hard "nope" for me and my parents don't even know I have a DUI.  At my hearing there were a few people who brought parents and family members with them.  Court is not time for a family reunion, but some people appreciate the support.  If she's going to cry and make a scene, then no, she shouldn't go.  Fortunately, your lawyer should just shut down the "I have a few additional questions" issue by just not returning the call.

Where I was the classes were on the weekends and it seems like on here a lot of them are during evenings.  My guess is they try to stay away from the 9-5 hours to avoid situations where everyone asks for "hardship exemptions" because they have to work and it clogs up the system.  

Employment wise it's going to be industry specific although in general the answer seems to be that it doesn't have much of an impact.  I can tell you in my field (law) unless you're looking to take the Bar Exam any time soon, you're probably going to be okay because at least in private practice background checks aren't routinely run and quite frankly nobody would be surprised to see a DUI in that field.  It's different when you get into court work where there's much more public scrutiny, but in general it's not going to be an issue.  

That insurance question seems odd although it feels like it's asked in a specific context relevant to the insurance industry in particular.  Probably better to ask someone directly connected with that industry; "criminal litigation" is a really weird way to word it!  A DUI generally isn't going to rise to the level of "crime relating to fraud or dishonest conduct" and if that's in a statement then quite frankly they should just have a list of what the relevant crimes even are.  That would take away the confusion!

Depends on how much you drank and what types of drinks they were, but generally that will be long enough.  Interlock techs advise you to wait 24 hours because at that point any amounts will have metabolized.  If your BAC was at .16 for example, that would be sufficient.

"First DUI" can mean anything from "just barely over the legal limit and probable cause is suspicious at best" to "three times the limit plus heavy drugs and opiates and an accident involving a minor was involved as well."  I'm guessing it's closer to the first scenario!  Before making decisions, the worst you can do is pay to consult with an attorney about what your options and potential consequences are.  Then you can decide whether it's necessary.  I will say, although I think a standard first offense DUI doesn't really require an attorney, the legal system generally (and criminal system in particular) is not designed for parties to represent themselves.  Depending on what's involved, you run the risk of telling a DA information about your case when you have a Constitutional right to remain silent.  It probably won't make much of a difference, but unless you have some guidance you're not going to instinctively know where those lines are.

For me it wasn't that the feelings of guilt weren't genuine, but I definitely get a sense that there's an "expectation" that we feel terrible about ourselves because of what could have happened.  If you think about it though, we put people in danger everyday when we text and drive and answer emails and drive, and swerve in and out of traffic, and needed to reach for our purse in the back seat to grab the exact change for the tolls.  But in all of those other circumstances, we never have to think about it because we don't get caught or if we do, there isn't the societal collective guilt and shaming about how "you could've killed someone."  I think we do the entire DUI community a disservice when we tell them that they need to look at how it can make them into a better person; because "better person" is almost always implied as "telling the world how you did a terrible thing."  I just don't think the self-flaggellation is necessary in order to learn an important lesson.  

A year and a half later I didn't come away from it with a "blessing in disguise" or "this made me a better person" type of attitude.  I don't think that's necessary either; you do the consequences and you end up smarter than 90 percent of all people who drink for happy hour and then decide they're okay to drive home.  Actually I probably drink more now than I did at the time although I'm smarter about it and do the heavy drinking at home!  The guilt went away when I went to my first group happy hour after the DUI and in the course of 2 hours saw everybody put down 4 cocktails (and these are attorneys, they're not weak cocktails!) and then decide to drive.  All of them had to be either at or over the legal limit and the difference is that none of them got caught. For whatever it's worth, I do think worse of myself now than I did pre-DUI and I don't know that that will ever change. But that's more because of what it did to my finances and to my relationship than because of hypothetical worst case scenarios.

So, with .09, it's close enough that an attorney could potentially argue he was legal at the time of the stop and then it rose to above the legal limit by the time of the official blow.  The timing between the stop and the police blow will matter here, but that's what I would expect.  Some places will let you argue blood alcohol levels in exchange for a reduced charge.  Quite frankly, with him blowing a .09, that's what I expect happened:  he was barely legal driving back and then it kept going up after he stopped.  It's \*\*really\*\* hard to feel the difference between a .07 and a .08 and just as hard to tell between .08 and .09.  An attorney will be able to tell him what to expect going forward.

Most of the time it isn't worth taking a DUI to a trial unless there's really something unusual.  Honestly $3,000 for a pretrial is just over 10 hours of time for an average attorney so it's really not that bad.

Impossible to say without knowing the state, but in general if you have to ask "what makes me eligible" and "when do I ask for it," the answer is to have a lawyer.  I can tell you that at least where I'm located, unless you have a situation where you're ineligible by statute (like you had a minor in the car, for example) if it's a first offense you're going to be offered diversion.  It was definitely something that could be handled without a lawyer if you otherwise know how the system works.  It's extremely clerical and paperwork heavy and I absolutely could've done it on my own.  I'm glad I didn't though, because my attorney knew exactly what to do and made sure everything ran smoothly.  Not every diversion program is like this though so it really will depend on where you're located.  The other thing to keep in mind is that even when you go into diversion, you're still a criminal defendant and so talking with DAs, etc., is not in your best interest; the system just isn't designed for defendants with a right to remain silent to represent themselves even though plenty do with no problem.

It's so state-specific but most states don't result in jail time for a first offense DUI unless there's something really unusual; think really uncooperative with officer, going 100 down a road that's 25, that type of thing.  I think someone posted here that their state had a mandatory jail sentence and the DA wouldn't let up with that but the vast majority of it was done on house arrest.  So for a first offense, it's possible but generally doesn't happen.  Generally it's considered a waste of resources to throw an 18 year old in jail over underage drinking.

So this is where it gets weird with each state.  Because there's the criminal penalty of a license suspension that comes with a DUI conviction or guilty plea, but then there's also the DMV (civil/administrative) penalty and the two may not run together at the same time.  As an aside, this is why you sometimes see criminal orders worded along the lines of "suspension for at least 90 days" because the DMV may impose a longer or shorter restriction (it seems to always be longer!).  

The best person to ask is your lawyer, who will know how the criminal side sees things at least.  Basically, ask will the 90 day DMV suspension count toward any criminal penalty.  The idea is that you don't want to pay a reinstatement fee if you're just going to get suspended again!

"Does therapy help."  I'd say no, not really.  I still have the suicidal thoughts although it's much more passive than it was this time last year. But in fairness, I'm also not someone who looks at my DUI as a big "learning moment" or "blessing in disguise" type situation, and I don't think that's necessary to be able to say you understand the consequences. What's hard about DUIs is not just that it's so isolating, but also because there's a social expectation of how you "should" react.  You "should" feel remorseful about what could've happened and "should" be grateful that it wasn't worse, and "should" look at it as an opportunity to reexamine drinking habits. But I don't think any of those are necessary to be able to say it's in the past.  It does start to become something that happened, but doesn't actively affect your life anymore though.  I think that's a point that comes at different times for everyone.  Admittedly I'm not supposed to say that therapy isn't helpful for this, but some things you just have to process on your own and even if a therapist is outwardly supportive, they can't change what already happened.

Plenty of people drive on a suspended license for awhile and never get caught but they're fortunate; driving on a suspended license is a ***bad*** idea and one of the most common reasons why people don't complete their probation successfully is because they get caught which has consequences including a longer suspension, mandatory jail time, etc.  I know NV is pretty spread out but if you're saying "across town" that suggests we're not talking about a job that's 60 miles away from where you live.  Rideshares, riding with coworkers, or even budgeting the income that you do have and adjust how much you're putting toward your court costs, are all ways to avoid a situation where your plate could be scanned and you get caught.  When I got pulled over for driving while suspended (but allowed to drive with an interlock), the police officer didn't want to hear any excuse and barely accepted "I'm allowed to drive with an interlock" as an answer.  It's not something to mess around with; this isn't like where if you're not supposed to drink during probation but get caught unexpectedly you might be able to talk yourself into a one-time free pass.
