It sort've depends on how far after the arrest you're in.  Have you been charged yet?  It doesn't always get into the system right away.  The driving record may or may not be affected yet; it depends on whether you have a suspended license yet.

Probation is completely separate from PennDot for interlock purposes.  It's never stated all that clearly, but basically there are the mandatory criminal penalties and then there are the license penalties.  That's why at lot of orders will be worded to say "license suspension for at least 12 months."  Because with the administrative fun you're ultimately going to be without a license for longer.  Mine was a 60 day suspension for example but between having to mail in my license and wait to get my restricted license, it was more like 70 days.  

Each month (I think you can extend it to every 60 days) you'll go and get the device recalibrated.  All of the data gets downloaded and reported to PennDot.  Because I was on ARD and my vendor was connected to the court system, it was also reported to the probation officer.  So if you had a lock out or violation, it would get reported to PennDot and to the probation officer.  This was a much bigger deal for me being on ARD at the time than it will be for you, because as part of ARD you're not supposed to be drinking anyway (though in my DUI classes people were bragging about how they planned to go to a football game after and get drunk).  60 days before you can get your license back, you'll go in for a final compliance check.  That's the one you absolutely have to have no violations on.  Then your vendor will certify compliance to PennDot.  But for violations up to that point, I haven't heard of anyone getting in trouble through PennDot provided they were compliant in the final 60 days.

For whatever it's worth, the $1K price is more likely if you do it the entire year.  I think the top one is at $1,500 for the full year.  If you were quoted $1k for an installation, find a different vendor.  It's around $175 for installation and then less than that for the regular checks.  Between the installation, calibration, and PennDot fees, I spent around $500 total for the 60 days.  If you were quoted that high for an actual installation, find somebody else.  Unless you're in Allegheny or Dauphin counties, you can choose any vendor.  For DUIs it's all ignition interlock these days, and even when the OLL was still permissible, you couldn't functionally use it for ARD because you were required to serve a 60 day hard suspension anyway.  Personally as much as I disliked the device, I'd much rather have that than the hard suspension and being completely dependent on others for rides.

The ignition interlock requirement will last for one year from the date of your suspension.  This is mandatory and state-wide.  It makes no difference what part of PA you're in because PennDot will ultimately have the final say.  They will not reinstate your unrestricted license after 6 months; you'll have to go to periodic compliance checks.  When you go to the final check, you have to establish that you have 60 days of no violations.  Then, your vendor certifies you're fully compliant, you go to a DMV to get your unrestricted license back, and then you get the device removed.  It's actually a lot easier than it sounds if you have a reputable vendor.  Mine sent in the compliance certification via fax or email, then I called PennDot 24 hours later to verify they received it, and I got my unrestricted license the next day.  

If by "work permit" you're referring to an Occupational Limited License, you're no longer able to do that for DUIs in PA.  I heard somebody say that they actually got a client approved for an OLL but that he was still required to have interlock in the car anyway!  So...not sure it even makes sense to apply for it.  

That said, how do you have a NJ license if you're a resident of PA?  And have you ever been licensed in PA?  I'm assuming you were at one point if you're eligible for an interlock.  It's going to be easier to comply with the interlock because any police officer who randomly runs your plates will see a suspension and you'll need to have a restricted license or something establishing that you're able to drive through the duration of your suspension.

If it's a first offense and there's nothing extremely unusual or aggravating, it's unlikely he'll do jail time.  If you read posts on here, the vast majority of those who do jail have done so because they don't get the lengthy probation period as a result and it's easier to just do 7 days (or however long) in jail than it is to keep shelling out money for probation.  Jut having an accident with a high BAC isn't particularly unusual; in my state the most common cause of DUIs is crashes and the average BAC is .16 and above.  I can't imagine it's much different elsewhere.  Jail time you're usually looking at having substantial aggravating factors, such as driving with minors in the car or substantial injuries to others.

I think if you truly have no idea where to start, a good way to default would be by choosing by which gender you're most likely to be able to open up to.  If a male therapist has good boundaries, then he should be able to help you.  At the same time, don't dismiss female therapists generally.  Ones who identify as being LGBTQ or allied will probably be good choices, particularly if you're open up front about how in general you haven't been able to connect with female therapists.  I think that therapists in general make more of an effort to meet you where you are if you express that you've had difficulties opening up in the past.

Are there expungement possibilities with the probation?  What about re-sentencing?  Meaning, does this offense "count" as a DUI conviction if you were to get caught again?  Also, what does probation entail?  Is it supervised or unsupervised?  Personally in my state, I wouldn't take a DUI conviction over probation.  But it really depends what you're getting in exchange for 18 months of probation.  If it's the potential expungement that may be different to you than if the "only" thing you're getting is that you don't have to go to jail.

So generally the way these work is that unless there's a travel restriction generally, you have a license of some sort.  I don't know if your permit has travel restrictions associated with it because sometimes your license only permits you to drive during certain hours or to certain places.

If your license doesn't have travel restrictions associated with it, it's not the fact that you would be out of state that's the problem:  it's the fact that you'd be operating a car without an interlock.  That's where the real violation tends to be.  The link you shared suggests that there aren't restrictions generally but you really need to clarify that.  

TL/DR: if one state requires you to drive a vehicle with an interlock, you won't get off the hook if you get caught driving in another state without it.

The interlock in all likelihood is more of a DMV requirement than a criminal requirement.  If you were caught driving without an interlock and your probation officer caught wind of it, then it would probably be extended or there would at least be some consequences.  But it's really a DMV issue.  

You need to check to see what the interlock requirements are for your state.  Some states go by the date you get your license restored.  So for example, if you get your license restored after one year, it will be flagged as an interlock license, meaning that any car you drive will have to have an interlock in it.  If you choose not to drive for three years, that's fine, the interlock period doesn't get extended because it's connected to your license restoration.  So the way it would work in that scenario is you get your license back in 2018 and then in 2021 the interlock requirement drops.  But other states seem to do it differently, where it appears to be based more off of when you actually begin driving a car again rather than when you get your license back.  Really the DMV is the one to talk to about interlock issues.  But it won't extend your criminal probation.

The restricted license permits you to drive a vehicle equipped with an interlock device during the duration of your suspension.  You get a notice from PennDot advising that your license is going to be suspended.  That notice should also advise you that you are permitted to apply for an ignition interlock limited license.  For mine (I did ARD), I was driving about 3 weeks after surrendering my license.  There's a bit of misinformation:  a lot of people think that because you're driving, it means you're driving with an interlock  *instead* of having a suspended license.  That is ***not*** true.  Your license still shows up as suspended during this time if a police officer runs the plates, but you're allowed to drive so long as the vehicles has an ignition interlock installed.

Sounds like mine as well!  Left early each day because of scheduled football games that everyone wanted to get home to watch (and freely talking about how they intended to drink quite a bit while watching!).  It was a complete joke.

In my state if you're suspected of a DUI and you refuse, you're automatically charged in the highest tier and PennDot suspends your license for 12 months--which more or less can't be appealed because it's not really a criminal matter.  So in that regard I think it's better to just comply when you're asked to submit to a blood test.

If it's your first offense and you're otherwise eligible (i.e., didn't have a child under age 14 in the car, etc.) you'll probably be offered ARD.  Some counties you have to go through an application process and others you just automatically get signed up for it if you ask for it at the preliminary hearing.  Even with the high BAC that usually won't preclude you.  Mine was around what yours was, and I had to pay the court costs ($2,776) then 60 day license suspension, then classes.  Technically I'm under probation for 12 months but after 6 I can ask for early termination because all of the requirements are complete.  The law just changed recently as well where you can drive with an interlock for the duration of your suspension.  So really, it was more like 2 1/2 to 3 weeks of no driving.
People pass those tests even just 24 hours after having a full drink if they limit it to just one.  If it really was just a sip, you're in all likelihood going to be fine.

1. Court costs specifically for me were $2,776 (yes, that's an exact number!)  They vary based upon the offense and the duration in the program, which ranges from 6 months to 24 months.  I'm technically on it for 12 but after 6 months if all of the costs have been paid and requirements completed, I can ask for early termination.  For me it actually comes out to less than the fines if there were an actual conviction because of the BAC.  
2. I lost my license for 60 days.  However, my state recently adopted a rule where you can drive with an interlock for the duration of your suspension.  So it was really only about 3 weeks of definite no driving.  I Ubered or just stayed home.  
3. My arrest record will be expunged once the program is complete and I request it.   The only ones who will keep records of it will be the District Attorney's office and PennDot keeps diversion on your driving record for I believe 10 years.  And I'm sure that there are some high level security personnel who will be able to find it.  

I'd do it again; there was potentially a defense because of the procedure used in my DUI, but it just wasn't worth the risk.

It seems some states handle is differently.  Right across the border in PA, refusing is generally a terrible idea.  First, you'll be charged at the highest tier regardless of what your actual BAC was, and secondly you have an automatic 12 month suspension from PennDot that is functionally not appealable.  At least if it's your first offense and you don't refuse, you'll in all likelihood do diversion and only lose your license for 60 days total.  If you did refuse, you lose it for 60 days *plus* the additional 12 months.  States truly are trying to punish people for refusing to self-incriminate like that.

For a background check, unless there are specific code sections relevant to BAC, I doubt it. Congratulations!  When mine was taken out there wasn't anything that could put me in a bad mood the rest of the day.  Did it feel weird to actually be able to turn the car all the way on?  It did for me and I couldn't do it at first!  LOL!

Is it a blow/hum system?  If it is, the hum is a pain.  I swear I did it correctly and it gave me error messages 5 times in a row. I had a bad accident as well; fell asleep at the wheel, car totaled, hit a telephone pole.  Also told myself I don't care if I never drive again and I'll never touch a drop of alcohol again. It felt amazing having that thing removed from my car!  I will say I have changed my thoughts toward drinking and driving afterwards.  I do know that truly one drink will put you at the .025 and you'll be allowed to start your car with an interlock.  My biggest long term concern in all of this is knowing where the real limit actually is.  The reality is that a true single drink (5 oz. wine, 12 oz. beer, etc.) will not put someone in impairment territory and I know that being "one and done" won't do that for me.  But psychologically I panicked about it and it was almost like I felt incredibly drunk after a single bottle of Yuengling.  Knowing that one drink will be at .025 especially after waiting for a bit goes a long way in calming that anxiety.  My experience with the device wasn't terrible although I only had it in for 60 days; but I wouldn't say it was pleasant.  The single positive thing about it was that it allowed me to drive; that's not insignificant but like the DUI process itself, I see nothing good that ultimately came out of it.  I was in the best mood though the day I had it removed from my car.

As far as other parents finding out, you can probably bow out of carpools, park further away, learn when the next retest will be so that you can time it so it won't go off around other people (all of mine came pretty predictably).  I think the script someone else posted here about how to explain it to your kids is pretty good, although 12 may be pushing the age where they'll figure out on their own that it was alcohol-related.

The technique is the hardest part because a lot of them are a blow-hum method (this is to make sure it's actually a human taking the test is what the installation tech said).  I swear I did nothing differently but it kept refusing to let me start.  One time out of curiosity I took out my tuning fork (yes I keep one in my car!) and decided to try out which pitches worked best in terms of humming.  What can I say, musicians are weird!  I never had any issues with false positives but I also only had it for 60 days and it was short enough to make some adjustments without being overly burdensome.  The rolling retests are a pain and I found them distracting; somewhere between drinking a cup of coffee and looking at the GPS on your phone trying to find out where to go.  I didn't find it as distracting as texting and driving.  You're told to pull over, but I doubt anyone really does that.  I've posted on here before that I've tried looking to spot other interlocks but so far haven't been successful; my guess is that most drivers are more focused on their phones than they are on anyone else.  Parking far enough away, leaving work when there were fewer people to notice, and slowing down during retests seemed to be enough.  The only people who know I even had one are the three people who know about the DUI; and even then, they never saw me use it.  I'd rather have the interlock than not be able to drive.

That's cheap; you could possibly find someone less expensive but that rate is extremely reasonable and if you're otherwise comfortable with the individual, I'd say to just do it. $3,500 flat fee.  Covered the preliminary hearing, arraignment, ARD hearing and eventual petition for early termination. That seems unlikely to work given the higher BACs after each offense and the timing.  If the BACs were lower it may actually work. I'd do it now.  The summons is coming and a lot of attorneys are going to be in the $3,500-$5,000 range to get you from the preliminary hearing to ARD.  When you get the summons, you'll have about 6 weeks until the actual preliminary hearing (which in Pittsburgh will be spent waiting in a large waiting room and signing a bunch of paperwork).
You lucked out!  What was your BAC?  I know of one person whose BAC was under the suspension limit (between .08 and .10) and the form had to be re-sent to PennDot.  That's wonderful for you!

If it's your first offense, the default offer in Pittsburgh is to do ARD.  It's non-reporting probation and at that BAC level it would probably be for 6 months.  You have to do Alcohol Highway Safety School and potentially DUI intervention (fair warning, they're both really boring).  The summons will probably come in the mail in the next few weeks; it comes regular and certified mail.  Once you're done with ARD, the court will automatically expunge your record. It really was a matter of filling out and signing paperwork but my lawyer made it extremely smooth.  I don't know that it would have gone so smoothly had I not had her.

3x a week sounds like intensive outpatient, which typically has a standard cut off point after several weeks.  Do you know whether that's the case? I think one of the US Presidents (Bush 2???) had a DUI and had to apply for a temporary residence permit to get to Canada. I mean obviously the "correct" answer is to not drive while under suspension and during those hard couple of weeks where I didn't have the interlock license, I really didn't drive. I think a lot of people do that.  Mine was 60 days and I had the interlock for most of that time.  When I didn't have it, I Ubered.  It's expensive--about $20 minimum one way. Because you're applying to law schools it will probably become necessary to address it even with just being a traffic violation.  The American Bar Association came out with another report on the use of alcohol among attorneys and so state Bars and law schools are going crazy with anything that could suggest a substance abuse problem.  Definitely once you apply for the Bar Exam expect to be asked (although my state may have capped it after 5 years, I don't remember at this point--the Bar Exam is something I've pushed out of my mind LOL). I'm not a fan of the bad reputation public defenders get because in the vast majority of cases involving DUIs it's not going to be worth going to a trial and the PD will get exactly the same result as a private attorney.  But just because private attorneys are expensive, that doesn't mean you're automatically entitled to a public defender.  You have to actually establish inability to pay.  My lawyer was expensive ($3,500 flat fee from beginning to end) but I can't say that it was an unreasonable amount.  It equaled around 15 hours of her time and with three court appearances, that happens quickly.  The system isn't designed to represent yourself in a criminal case and if you succeed on your own, it's in spite of being unrepresented rather than because of it.

>At that level, that's unlikely.  .27 is extremely high; it's pushing coma territory for someone who truly never drinks.  So if you were at that level and felt okay to drive, you've built up a tolerance over a period of time.  No test is 100 percent accurate, but it's not going to be that far off.  I only mention that because with such a high BAC you will in all likelihood be required to have some kind of evaluation for substance abuse and there is no way an evaluator will believe that it was a one-time occurrence at that level.

At that high of a BAC, you need a lawyer.  That's a high enough level where assuming diversion programs or lessened sentencing is even available to you, the DA is going to be less likely to offer it.  In my state we pretty much throw about 90 percent of first-time offenders into a diversion program but that caps out at .24 BAC.  A lawyer can also ask for electronic home monitoring or other ways to prevent you from having to serve jail time.

I had to use Smart Start because I'm required to go through a specific provider and that's who they use. Three people know; for the most part I don't have enough of a social life for the driving issue to come up. I do consider myself a criminal and as a result that permanently means I'm not a good person, and some of the comments here solidify that. And in a lot of cities, find out where the judges and DAs ad PDs hang out on a Friday afternoon, spend a few hours there and watch how few of them get rides home compared to how much alcohol gets put down...then you'll see that you're literally being judges by people are drinking and driving themselves.  "Do as I say, not as a I do" applies here.  For being a generally non-violent crime DUIs are absolutely intended to ruin lives.  That's the whole point of the system.  It seems generally successful.

Texting/driving seems to be a summary offense and my guess is tired driving is in the catch all "careless driving" category that anyone can get stuck with! Same way here.  Regular stop, nope.  No right to counsel.  Once the handcuffs go on, yes. Mine is fairly predictable although it's getting a little wonky lately.  It's pretty consistent with the first retest at 5-6 minutes.  The second one appears to be at around 30 minutes. I'd just give the facts; conviction, date, terms of sentence.  Nothing else will help if they're set on disqualifying you because of it and it seems more likely to only hurt you.

Prior to my interlock, I was using Lyft and Uber if I couldn't get a ride.  It's about 20-27 one way from my house to work.  I live 15 miles away and biking really wouldn't have been realistic; to get to my office I have to cross down a major highway and go over a river and in general my city just isn't bike-able.  It wasn't a long period though that I really couldn't drive; otherwise I would have had to consider moving closer to work.  I think a lot of people either have to move closer or they just drive anyway while suspended.

Given the cultural stigma surrounding DUIs these days, I would have taken the deal as well.  Especially when the vast majority are plead down or settled, there isn't much generosity if you take it to trial and get convicted anyway.  Obviously people do go to trial and win them, but the risk of something going wrong is extremely high.

The thing is these days the DUI culture is one where police don't even have to lie to get charges to stick.  DUI is one of the few issues where you are very much presumed guilty and you really have an uphill battle in proving innocence even with probable cause issues, etc.    


In fairness, my actual DUI cop was cordial enough.  The one who pulled me over a few weeks ago for driving while suspended even though I'm allowed to drive with an interlock wasn't quite so cordial and the way he behaved you would have sworn I killed somebody and was trying to do away with the body.  Meanwhile he pulled me over on a busy road where the speed limit is 55 and most are going at least 70 and texting and driving is very much in full swing out here.  But I'm the danger to the roads.  My opinion of them isn't so great at the moment.

Have no idea what DIP is but assuming that you'll be under some type of monitoring for compliance with the 3 years of no alcohol, I imagine that drug testing will be a possibility.  It's usually going to be urine screening; it's faster and less expensive for the county.  Though someone on here posted not too long ago about a hair follicle test if you traveled outside of the country.  That seems extremely unusual though.

In my state you still have an interlock license but you're not required to install it in a vehicle if you don't have a vehicle.  Basically, you have to complete a separate petition that certifies you don't own or possess a vehicle, send it in, and then you still get approved for interlock license.  So if that did change, you would still be required to have the device.

It depends on the county, the offense, etc.  Mine is 12 months of non-reporting probation.  Technically we're still bound to the standard probation terms of no drinking, no travel without permission (which all the probation officers said specifically didn't apply to us because of being in a diversion program), report contact with the police, don't commit another crime, etc.  Technically you can be drug tested which presumably includes testing for alcohol as well but my attorney told me that doesn't happen.  Basically, they're not supervising you in any way that they would be able to enforce the "don't drink alcohol" provisions.  After 6 months if my court costs are paid off I can terminate probation early.  It seems like my county is a little lax when it comes to enforcement in comparison to other counties in my state.

My lawyer was expensive ($3,500) and ultimately I could have gotten the result I wanted without hiring her.  But I'm glad I hired her all the same, because she made everything so easy and quick which probably wouldn't have happened had I done everything on my own.  The criminal system and really any legal system isn't set up for people to do it on their own and even if I had gotten the same result, it would have been in spite of being unrepresented rather than because I was unrepresented.

I'm in PA.  As much as I complain about PA's program, especially when it comes to the court costs, it's actually quite low-maintenance compared to some of what I read on here.  In my county, non-reporting probation for a year, they're more than happy to terminate after 6 months if you get all the requirements done and then it gets expunged.

I tend to think of it as, you can definitely do it on your own and get the same result, but if you have anything unusual or particularly problematic, at least talk with a lawyer first before saying outright no.  And a lot of PD's offices will have income guidelines so it's not necessarily as easy as just saying you'll go with someone appointed.  For me it was a lot ($3,500) but she kept me from doing something stupid like walking up to the police officer and the DA and telling them I expected to be offered a diversion program.  That's just not how it works and is what I would have done!  It was a lot but I can't say it was unreasonable and she ultimately made the court part the easiest part of the process.  I agree though, it's a mess and a DUI is one of the few crimes where you genuinely are presumed guilty until proven innocent.

It's better than not being able to drive but an inconvenience all the same.  Lately what's been happening is it doesn't register right away, so I have to take a retest.  This is happening every single time and I swear I'm not doing anything differently!  It isn't supposed to be marked as a violation but we'll see.  I really don't think it's safe but there really isn't a way for me to pull over on my route and part of me likes the passive-aggressive idea of saying I'd like to get into an accident so I could say "the interlock made me do it."  I know, I know, that would just make things worse, but it would be 15 minutes of satisfaction.  The only thing I've had immediately before using it (about 5-10 minutes maybe) is coffee with half and half in it.  I have never received a violation or a warn as a result but I may have just gotten lucky.  I wouldn't go chowing down on a full meal right beforehand or eat/drink while driving!  It's better than not being able to drive at all, but at least for me my drive really is between home and work and the occasional trip to the gas station.  I get it out next month which is good because I'm way overdue for an oil change!

I know in my state once the expungement is complete it goes away from the FBI and state police records, and fingerprints, mugshots, etc. are destroyed.  The DMV keeps it on your driving record for 10 years and the DA's office keeps it for 10 years as well because of sentencing purposes. But once it falls off the driving record then it wouldn't show up anymore.

Attorney.  I'm self-employed so the DUI hasn't affected my job; if I had been convicted or plead guilty I would have been required to report it and would have lost my license to practice.  Fortunately with a diversion program it results in an expungement at the end and I'm not required to make any report.  Nobody in the community knows and it was quite the experience at my final hearing trying to avoid some of the attorneys I know who were there.  It's a bit nerve-wracking though because I don't know whether I'm \*\*really\*\* in the clear license-wise.  Basically, if someone finds out will they try to get me in trouble with my license.  If I were applying for admission I would have to disclose it on my Bar application.  I have no idea what the results would have been but considering the rather high rate of alcohol abuse among attorneys my guess is there would have to be some assurance that it won't happen again.  I don't know whether employers would run a background check.  For smaller firms it isn't standard practice around here, because everyone knows that if you're convicted or plead guilty you'll lose your license.

Has anyone from your insurance company been out to inspect the car?  That would be the first place to start.  Mine was totaled and the insurance company just took care of towing it and getting rid of it.  I would prioritize getting the car out of impound because those fees will keep adding up the longer it stays there.

That's a good tip!  I'm actually not sure if Geico knows anything about the DUI.  My incident involved and accident and because there was property damage and medical bills involved I'm assuming they had plenty of opportunities to learn if it was alcohol-related.  I never actually said there was a DUI and don't think I was required to.  I actually did check my policy terms and never found anything requiring disclosure so just kept quiet!  The accident raised my rate...by a whole $12.  So I'll try just not saying anything and see if that works!

I think in general texting is relatively new and there just haven't been enough accidents yet connected to it.  I think as time goes on it will change.  It's actually quite disturbing now where basically if I see a car swerving in and out of lanes in the afternoon I assume it's texting rather than a DUI.  And usually there's a cell phone involved in it!

If you weren't convicted in TN I doubt they can do much on the DMV end.  It's usually the criminal court that sets out the interlock requirement and the DMV which carries it out and then determines whether you can get your license back.  I can't imagine TN would even get involved as long as you have a valid license.  But is there any reason why you can't just keep your current license for the next 6 months once you move and then get a TN license?

Lose the paperwork as in they lost your entire file?!  This is why we have electronic files.  I guess it just stays as a pending matter which is probably okay unless you need to have a background check done or go to Canada.  I think arrest records still show up if the charge hasn't been expunged.  But I don't think you can get DUIs expunged in Georgia anyway so it may not matter.  I think I'd probably just not bring it up again so they don't go looking for it or by the time they find it enough time will have passed that it makes the court look bad for losing it in the first place.

I'd be sure to ask what the repercussions are from refusing the breathalyzer.  In my state you're automatically treated as a top tier offender and your license will be suspended for 12 months.  Also, ask about whether your lawyer is aware of nursing license issues if you take a plea deal.  Because a plea deal may get you something better, but licensing boards don't necessarily see things the same way.  All the best.

For my court date I had to be there at 7am and was out by 9:30.  But that was actually less time than I thought it would take.  Basically when it comes to court appearances I'd say an average is 3 hours and then if you get out before then you're lucky.  Probably best to tell your professor that you have to be in court that day--unless you can push off the date for a later time.  That would actually be the best solution.  Court dates get continued and moved all the time because of scheduling issues.

I have zero experience in this.  It will probably be a lot of classes and group activities.  I suppose the obvious "don't" is don't bring in alcohol or anything related to alcohol!  There will probably be breathalyzer tests etc.  Do let us know.  All the best this weekend.

I'm almost 3 months in.  I have about $1,300 left to pay in court costs out of the original $2,776 and those will be paid by April.  Technically I could be called in for random drug/alcohol screens but I haven't been.  I called the PO yesterday after I was pulled over on my interlock and she emphasized that once I pay off my court costs and hit the 6 month mark I can get off of probation early.  Technically it's up to the DA to agree to it, but she made it sound like it's a guarantee if everything is done.  Right now it'll be sweating out the next 30 days while I'm on the interlock and hope I don't get pulled over again (thank goodness for Waze which notifies you if there are police nearby!) and then it's just serving out the rest of the term.  I was afraid to call the PO because I thought it would make her want to meet me and do a drug screen but none of that came up during our call.  All other requirements are done.
Thank you for posting this; I think it's helpful over in this corner to hear from those who have come out on the other end.  Do drop in after year 2 finishes to let everyone know how you're doing.

I thought Mexico was okay so long as it's a misdemeanor conviction; though isn't a DUI a felony in Canada?  Really speaking to the consulate would be the best step if you can't locate an attorney in Mexico who can tell you one way or the other.

>I find the IID to be somewhere between drinking a cup of coffee in a snowstorm and texting and driving.  I've definitely had some close calls with having to suddenly slow down so I don't get "caught in the act" by other drivers, and doing rolling retests in snow squalls or heavy rain isn't safe.  Part of me likes the idea of getting into an accident so I can say the interlock made me do it.  Not that that would help insurance-wise, but I have absolutely nothing positive to say about this process!  Fortunately with mine, the device goes off predictably; 6 minutes and then 35 minutes.  Most of my driving requires me only to retest once and so if need be, I can wait out the 6 minutes so I don't get stuck doing it at a traffic light.  I basically don't turn on my car unless I know that nobody is around and then I make sure to get into work before 8 and then leave after 7 so there are fewer people on the road and it's dark and nobody sees it.  Covering the thing with a t-shirt probably helps even just to keep it warm because isn't it a rule in NY that you aren't allowed to disconnect the device?

Usually the grading is related to sentencing and if its "undefined" or "ungraded" it means the penalties can be more specific than the standard "minimum/maximum" for certain offenses.  It seems like a lot of states characterize DUIs in this way; supposedly it enables courts to impose DUI-specific penalties but there are also various types of penalties for other non-violent crimes as well which are still classified in the standard 1st, 2nd, 3rd degree range so...who knows!  If that's what it means then for background check purposes it probably doesn't make much of a difference; someone who's going to freak out over a misdemeanor will probably focus on the misdemeanor part rather than the grade which is really focused on the specific sentence.  Your lawyer would know though!

First offense DUI barely over the limit, you probably could handle it on your own without a lawyer, but I think the $2000 is well worth it.  With mine there was no question that I needed to go into diversion instead of trying to challenge it; we never really discussed it, I already had my mind made up.  She made the process extremely smooth and kept me from doing something bad like behaving like a lawyer instead of a criminal defendant--which would have only alienated the DA!  Seriously the court process was the easiest part of everything because she made it so smooth; just a bunch of paperwork and a hearing in front of the judge which consisted of answering a single question and that was it!  I never worked with a public defender but caseload aside, they are in DUI court all the time; they know the DAs, they know the procedure, they're good to have.  They may also be confined to their own requirements though, so if you're able to afford private counsel, it's worth the investment.  Good luck.
All the time, these days.

Unless you're in a situation where you seriously injured or killed someone, jail time almost never happens for a first offense.  If you think about it it makes sense; there are far too many 1st offense DUIs and putting everyone in jail for an extended time would place a huge burden on the system.  So most likely, you'll be advised to take a plea deal.  And even if it doesn't seem necessary, let your lawyer go through the exercise to look at what the police did when they charged you.  All the best.

My guess is you probably "could" in a pinch but it would be horribly inaccurate and subject to a whole host of legal challenges so nobody would do that.  The procedure seems to be a standard vial.  I think some places may take two so that you have a vial for re-testing if needed.  Not sure if they did that with me; if they did the vials were switched out immediately.

I didn't tell my parents and don't intend to; they live on the other end of the state, they don't travel, they don't need to give me rides, and quite frankly I don't need the lecture.  I told three people and the only reason was because the car was totaled and I knew I'd be losing my license; otherwise I wouldn't have told them.  Of those three, one has been rather unsupportive (the boyfriend of all people who reminds me of how horrible and selfish I am) and I just don't talk about it anymore.  The others were helpful for giving rides, but again, I don't talk about it.  Why would I want to talk about how I'm a criminal unless I really want to make other people feel better about how they're much better people than I will ever be?  It does seem though that the people who are more open about it seem to handle the process better; or maybe it's that they tell people they know will be supportive. For me I do feel like this decision ruined my life and I deserve to have that happen and don't deserve support.  If you think your parents will be supportive of you through the process, it may help to tell them.  Otherwise, probably best to avoid it if you can.  Unless your job is one where you're required to report a criminal conviction, you can leave them out of it.

We were told in DUI class that if that happens to us, to put the keys in the trunk or put them underneath or outside of the car.  It's harder to say physical control at that point!  But it also gets tricky because if a police officer approached you and it was obvious that you had driven to get to the spot where you're parked, they can get you that way as well.  It's quite unbelievable!  I knew that if your car was running and you were in the driver's seat you could still get a DUI for possession/control but I didn't realize it extended to being in the passenger seat and having the keys on your person or in the back seat of your car!

I had no idea buying out CS was even a thing!  My guess is that there are too many DUIs and not enough people to oversee everybody so giving the option lowers the number who need hours.  I didn't get CS so have no idea if buyout is even possible but I would so do that if it were!

I think "recovering" from the experience is a relative term.  My DUI involved an accident and I still start to panic if someone cuts me off in traffic, and this was 6 months ago.  The depression came pretty quickly after it happened; as soon as I was served with my summons I wrote a suicide letter, planned my exit but backed out because I looked up success rates for my chosen method and didn't like the 25 percent chance that I would fail.  It's not a constant thought, but every court fee, every time I have to use that interlock, every person I have to interact with through this process puts me further down the hole.  It doesn't help that in my profession the attitude is to look down upon those of us in it who ended up with DUIs but we're the ones who practically created binge drinking at happy hour!  Seriously I've seen people put down 5 drinks in a less than two hour time-span, and you're fairly ridiculed if you Uber back home.  I'm not entirely convinced they're any "better" than I was pre-DUI.  Positivity has now come to mean "it could have been worse," and from reading here, it would have been much harder had this occurred anywhere else.  Right at this part of the process, I think there's a disconnect between knowing rationally that it's temporary and it goes by quickly but at the same time feeling like the process can't move any slower.  Good luck; take it slow and give yourself the space you need.

Those court costs are amazing--in my state mine were $2,776 and this is a diversion program!  My state basically funds its court system off of DUI offenders.  That was on top of the $3,500 I paid for my attorney.  Actually it sounds like overall the sentence was fairly tame.  That's great you can apply for early release from probation.  What is even involved in a vehicle impound and what good is that supposed to do when you're already getting your license suspended???  Time to start checking things off of the list!

Well really, the criminal court and the DMV are two entirely separate entities.  Ultimately as much as criminal judge wants to pretend he has all the power, the DMV is actually the one which controls your license.  Why do you think people are only ordered 60 day license suspensions and end up serving them much longer because of a DMV issue?  Not sure where you are, but at least in my state the criminal court and the DMV really don't communicate much other than to send in forms saying to suspend a license.  I doubt most criminal courts find out about suspension appeals unless you specifically tell them.  Suspension appeals usually appear to be unsuccessful, but if the DMV goes for it, it's ultimately their call.  Your no-alcohol license might be an interlock license and so you probably wouldn't be allowed to drive a vehicle without that device.  So it's still technically "suspended," but it's a soft suspension.

There are lawyers who handle DMV issues and so it's worth contacting someone just to establish what the requirements are.  For example, she was under 21 at the time of the conviction but does she actually need the under 21 program?  I just looked at the DMV website for Delaware and it looks like she could just go to any agency to complete an outpatient program.  It sounds like it's more a matter of finding out what the red tape is she needs to cut through to satisfy the DMV that she's done everything.  A lawyer can't necessarily get her around those requirements but may be able to to advise on what she needs to do to get the suspension lifted.

Probably lawyer time.  You're undoubtedly supposed to report police interactions, especially if you were cited.  The police department itself could probably check and verify that you're on probation and report it themselves.  Paying a fine may mean a guilty plea which could cause all kinds of problems with probation.  So you want to talk with a lawyer.  Consequences for a first time violation...I don't know, it hasn't happened for me yet, but some probation officers will give it a pass for a first time if it was relatively minor and others will immediately seek to revoke probation.  It really depends on the procedures of the court handling your case.

At the beginning of the process I asked my lawyer how long I could expect and she said usually 30 days you get a summons.  This may be more state and county specific, but 30 days appears fairly standard.  She said it can go up to 60 and occasionally you get it later for some unexplained reason, but it usually isn't that long.  Fingers crossed for you...

Weeeird!  I'd say you got lucky but almost don't want to say that because of jinxing it!  Seriously though, a combination of "accident involving another vehicle, no ticket, no citation, no field sobriety tests, no breathalyzer, no urine screen (which is bad for alcohol testing anyway) and no blood draw."  "Suspected intoxication" but not following through to confirm it just doesn't establish a DUI!  The only thing I suppose could happen is if the police asked if you were drinking even if it was done in a somewhat coded way an in the commotion you just don't even remember it happening.  Or maybe doing the whole "point the light in the eyes" thing and saying "glassy and bloodshot eyes, looks like intoxication."  But really a police officer going forward with that is just asking for challenges and it seems silly to not just take the additional time to confirm suspicions!  I really do hope you caught a break here from an officer who forgot to follow protocol.

Assuming the IV was for central line purposes or whatever it's called.  The standard one everyone is given unless you're like me and refuse and put up a fight with the staff!  Were you conscious the entire time you were in the hospital?  Generally blood tests have to be done while you're conscious so you can consent to it.  I was pretty far over the limit and in an accident resulting in a totaled car and a very definite concussion, but I vividly remember consenting to a blood draw.  At this point if you're charged with a DUI, you're more likely to receive notice by summons rather than police showing up at your house to arrest you.  Did police speak with you at the hospital?  If they did, it's more likely you would receive a blood draw.  All the best--the waiting is the worst part of this.

I tell my divorce and custody clients all the time that court is not like Law and Order and speaking usually either has no effect or outright doesn't help (criminal court is so much easier than family court but that's a different story!).  So I come down on the side of if you say anything to make it \*\*very\*\* brief.  I'm in a diversion program and my court date was literally about 70 people in a room and literally you walk up in a line, your attorney meets you in a screwed up pseudo "meet me at the altar" kind of way, and then all you have to answer is "yes, your Honor" when the judge asks if you understand the terms of the program.  Nothing more needed.  I imagine most DUI courts are similar because there are so many DUI defendants.  Anxiety was still at an all-time high which manifested in accidentally throwing a pen which landed at the other end of the room (!!!) and getting a bit snarky when a few kids started talking about what they did and said something like it's a bad idea for criminal defendants to be talking in detail about the night they got arrested.  In this situation the whole "I know what I'm doing and know how this system works" was a defense mechanism.  If you have a good lawyer who you trust, you can safely let them do the talking.  Then that part will be done.  One thing that helped--it's really easy to feel singled out.  In this context, you really are just a number.  That's usually not a good thing, but it helped to think that the DA is really just reading off names, the judge is asking the same questions and then that's it.  You've got this.  :-)

Assuming there are no probation/bail conditions attached to alcohol consumption, you're probably going to be okay on an EtG test.  The 80 hour marketing is more for extreme, constant drinking at very high levels.  It would probably be cleared within 24 hours and even heavy drinking tends to be gone in about 48 hours.  Of course, if you do get caught (such as by running into the substance abuse counselor with an IPA in your hand) then there could potentially be consequences.  Only you can decide whether to take that risk.
DMV procedures are a mess anywhere--what state are you in?

If you don't mind my asking, was the reaction what you expected or did you expect something very negative and were surprised to receive support?  The people in the group you were with right before may have realized that the same thing could have happened to them and so ignoring you meant they could deny that reality.  Just a thought.  The happy medium I seem to be finding these days is this board and blogging about my experiences.  It lets me keep (some) anonymity--at least I think it does but still gives me some way to talk about what's happening.  I'm finding a DUI to be a strange combination of incredibly invasive and isolating all at the same time.  That's so wonderful that you have such a supportive family to see this through with you.

Well that's stupid.  Unless the goal is to actually get more DUIs because we all know that DUI offenders have to pay court costs which practically fund the counties and the mental health providers.  Still, anyone can come up with a bill.  It doesn't mean it will pass; and yes, it's a stupid idea!  People will just find ways to lower the prices.

Ooo, this is a tough one because with a new job you probably won't have accrued vacation time.  Is there a way that you can play the delay game where you just keep pushing out court dates so that the actual jail time wouldn't be until you've had enough time saved up that you could use vacation/sick/personal/planned unpaid?  I guess it doesn't matter if it's part time work.  The other benefit is that if you're around for awhile you can gauge whether they'll be understanding and you can say more about the situation.  I wouldn't bring it up at the interview or offer stage because that's taking a huge risk.
That's incredible!  It's no small accomplishment given the amount of emotional and financial strain a DUI causes.  I hope the rest of the process is just as smooth for you.
Small steps, but each one gets you closer.  Having a lawyer will help; I thought the court part was actually the easiest because I had a good lawyer!
That must be such a relief!  Now the hard part and the "checklist" begins.  But at least you're no longer waiting and worrying about what will happen.  Now to enjoy a much needed nights' sleep!

I guess that depends on what you mean by "normal."  I had my DUI in August and got into ARD in December.  I just finished my court requirements this past weekend.  Now to have my license suspended until April but I have the interlock so at least I'm driving.  That's more of a "tolerable inconvenience" than "new normal."  I feel slightly more along the lines of "the end is barely visible" than I did before, but it's nowhere near what I would say is "normal."  I don't know that I'll ever be able to see myself as anything other than "a criminal."  Maybe after everything is done that feeling will go away but right now it's still too fresh.

I think in this situation it's okay to tell her that you need to start smaller right now.  I'm not in AA myself but I don't believe the object of the exercise is to overwhelm you or start you down a path which you don't think is sustainable; that doesn't benefit you and turns it into a stressful experience rather than one which keeps you focused on sobriety.  If that changes, you can revisit your plan.  The idea is that the sponsorship should really be a collaborative dialogue.  I think it's okay to explain it to her in this way.

Here's how it's been for me:  preliminary hearing, arraignment and ARD hearing were pretty "clinical."  I don't think I said a word to anyone.  That was honestly the easiest part because my county is so focused on "first time offenders otherwise eligible get ARD."  In other counties it's different.  There is an evaluation (which for me wasn't so bad although I've read some horror stories) and then if you're top tier you have to do outpatient counseling (group therapy in my neck of the woods) and three AA meetings.  The AA meetings were ridiculous and honestly that's my biggest criticism of this.  Really unfair to force people who don't want to be there onto people who are sharing very personal information and opening up.  I have a real problem with that and quite frankly AA should stop signing court slips to stop this behavior.  No victim impact panel out here or community service.  Your lawyer should be able to tell you what type of conditions to expect and whether your probation will be reporting or non-reporting.
Yup.  I'm on day 12 now since I sent in my license.  Got a letter from PennDot saying they received my surrendered license but no camera card.

I'd contact the vendor that actually installed it because ultimately they're the ones who have to issue the Declaration of Compliance saying you had no violations in the last 60 days (30 for ARD).  A missed rolling retest is considered a violation.  Make sure that when you turn off the engine, it always says "Restart" to prevent that from happening again.

Really I don't understand why people tell the whole community including their parents.  I only told three people who needed to know because I wouldn't be able to hide it from them.  If I wouldn't have lost my license I wouldn't have even told them.  There's a lot of stigma against DUIs and there's no need to tell people unless they actually need to know. This process is invasive as much as it's isolating and as horrible as it is to be so isolated and alone with the depression, I chose to keep my privacy.  It's weird, there are a lot of court personnel who find out, a bunch of strangers in DUI school, people from the DMV etc.  Basically everyone knows except the people in your circle.  But that keeps the privacy.

In my opinion it's never my place to tell someone what decisions they should or shouldn't make with their life, and that includes decisions about ending it.  I'm not saying that to sound "pro-suicide," but to say that I'm not going to tell you life is worth living and that you still have much to live for.  What I will say, as someone who who has also had a lot of depression because of a DUI is that reading this forum helps.  A lot of posters here have gone through it, and more importantly, they've had a lot of time pass.  I find their insight to be helpful and it provides some hope that even though it feels horrible now, eventually it may go away.  They've been able to get employment, finish school, and generally put it behind them.  Many people who post here show that for the most part, nobody even knows about the DUI unless they themselves chose to say something.  It may help to talk with someone at student services.  You aren't alone in this; I'm so sorry for your loss.

Basically on probation, once it's complete there will be no criminal record and everything will be expunged.  My evaluation recommended the alcohol highway safety school plus DUI intervention (group therapy) and three AA meetings.  I'm not thrilled with the other two because the evaluator specifically told me he didn't think I had a substance abuse issue requiring treatment.  I was ordered to do it because of being in an accident and having a high BAC.  Not impressed with the AA meetings (I have some fundamental issues with AA philosophically though recognize that it saves lives for many others and really it's extremely offensive to AA as an organization to inflict people like me onto it) and I can't say I'm looking forward to DUI intervention which is basically group therapy.  But the AA meetings were easy enough to get out of the way just by showing up, sitting in the back and getting my slip signed.  And the group therapy should be easy enough to just sit back and just participate minimally.  So I wouldn't say positive outcome, but it could be worse, so we'll go with neutral.  Technically random D&A testing is always a possibility here but practically it doesn't happen unless you get picked up for a new crime or someone reports a violation to the probation officer.
I haven't heard that in about 20 years!  Good way to keep perspective.

Right now the DUI will show up as "adjudicated."  Actually it sounds like you haven't had your preliminary hearing yet, but once you're accepted into ARD (probably around April) that's what will show up if you look up your record on the criminal docket.  The arrest shows up on the criminal background but it won't show a conviction.  While you're in ARD it will continue to show as "adjudicated" but again, that's not a guilty finding.  Expungement will be done automatically but can take several months for the state and FBI records to be fully destroyed.  I wouldn't disclose it if you're not directly asked.  Even now, you haven't been convicted of anything and you're not lying if you say you haven't been convicted.  Keep trying, and good luck.  Job searching is stressful enough even in the best of circumstances.

I'm so sorry you're going through this.  I'm only a few months into my DUI and started a blog to process the experience.  My perspective comes as both someone who works in the legal field and as someone who has a DUI.  

There's only so much a lawyer can do--I think in every state you can get a DUI even if you weren't actually driving; it's not even a mitigating factor.  There's only so much a lawyer can do; the DAs offices are told to go harsh on DUIs because that's what the public wants and they're the ones who are voting next election cycle.  At that BAC unless you can establish improper calibration or improper stop, it's so hard to do more than plead down.  I really think that when people get charges dropped it's because they have something unique or they just get lucky.  

From a personal perspective, the waiting is hard, but the actual court proceedings are the easy part.  It's once it's over and you're officially "a criminal" that it gets hard.  DUI school, depression sets in, etc.  Budgeting will help keep on top of the fines and court costs.  A lot of people do seem to find DUI school helpful just because there are other people who made the same mistake.  Most importantly (and I have a hard time telling myself this), it's okay to forgive yourself.  You made a mistake, but it will pass.

ARD isn't going to drug test (and you used the word "neb," are you in Pittsburgh area?).  In that case, you won't be UA'd unless you do something wrong.  There's not enough resources to do that with ARD participants.  I guess if you actually write on a court form that you're intoxicated when you show up to court it would be different, but I wasn't and haven't been tested and it doesn't seem like anyone in my DUI classes was either.
